overview: Phonetics and Phonology (E410) explores the physical reality and abstract organization of speech sounds in human language, focusing especially on English (Received Pronunciation). The course begins by establishing the fundamental dichotomy between phonetics—the universal, physical study of speech production (articulatory), transmission (acoustic), and perception (auditory)—and phonology—the language-specific study of sound systems, phonemes, and functional contrasts. It examines classical and modern phonological theory through the seminal contributions of Nikolai Trubetzkoy, Roman Jakobson, Daniel Jones, Noam Chomsky, and Morris Halle. Students learn the classification and phonetic properties of all 44 English phonemes: 12 monophthongs, 8 diphthongs, 5 triphthongs, and 24 consonants analyzed by voicing, place, and manner of articulation. Moving to suprasegmental phonology and prosody, the course investigates the phonetic and phonological structure of syllables, the Sonority Sequencing Principle, and phonotactic constraints. It analyzes connected speech processes including strong versus weak forms, contractions, elision, and assimilation (regressive, progressive, coalescent). Suprasegmental phenomena are deepened through word stress rules, sentence stress, chunking into tone units (pre-head, head, tonic syllable, tail), tone types (fall, rise, fall-rise, rise-fall, level), and the multi-dimensional communicative functions of intonation (grammatical, attitudinal, discourse, accentual). Finally, practical competence is demonstrated through broad and narrow IPA transcription of connected speech, including linking and intrusive phenomena (/r/, /j/, /w/). This comprehensive foundation equips students to analyze spoken language critically for academic linguistics, ELT pedagogy, and oral viva voce defense.

topics.title: Phonetics and Phonology: Definitions, Differences, Classification, and Correlation
topics.coreIdea: Phonetics studies the concrete, physical properties of speech sounds universally, whereas phonology examines how sounds function systematically to distinguish meaning within a specific language. Understanding their differences and correlation reveals how physical phonetic data forms the raw material organized by abstract phonological rules.
topics.vivaAnswer: Phonetics is the universal study of the physical production, acoustic transmission, and auditory perception of speech sounds, transcribed in square brackets [ ]. Phonology is the language-specific study of how sounds function, pattern, and distinguish meaning in a mental linguistic system, transcribed in slashes / /.
topics.example: In English, [pʰ] (aspirated in 'pin') and [p] (unaspirated in 'spin') are two physically different phones studied in phonetics, but in phonology, both represent the single phoneme /p/ because the difference does not change word meaning.
topics.understandMore: Phonetics is traditionally divided into three branches: articulatory phonetics (how vocal organs produce sounds), acoustic phonetics (the physical properties of sound waves such as frequency, amplitude, and formants measured by spectrograms), and auditory phonetics (how the ear and brain perceive and decode sound signals). Phonetics and phonology are mutually dependent: phonetics provides the empirical raw material, while phonology provides the structural grammar and functional interpretation of that material.
topics.commonConfusion: Students often treat phonetics and phonology as synonyms or confuse their notations. Phonetics deals with concrete, physical sounds (phones) written in square brackets [ ], while phonology deals with abstract, psychological units (phonemes) written in slashes / /.

topics.title: Phonemes, Phones, Allophones, and Phonological Theory (Trubetzkoy, Jakobson, Jones, Chomsky, Halle)
topics.coreIdea: A phoneme is an abstract, meaning-distinguishing sound unit realized as concrete phones or contextual allophones. Phonological theory has evolved from structuralist functionalism and physical sound families (Trubetzkoy, Jones) through acoustic distinctive features (Jakobson) to generative rule-based derivations from underlying to surface representations (Chomsky and Halle).
topics.vivaAnswer: A phoneme is the smallest abstract contrastive sound unit that distinguishes meaning, proven via minimal pairs (e.g. /p/ vs /b/ in 'pat'/'bat'). Key theorists include Trubetzkoy (oppositions and neutralization), Jones (concrete phoneme and Cardinal Vowels), Jakobson (binary distinctive features), and Chomsky & Halle (generative phonology in SPE).
topics.example: In English, [pʰ] in 'pin' and [p] in 'spin' are in complementary distribution—they never contrast in the same environment and therefore function as allophones of the phoneme /p/.
topics.understandMore: Trubetzkoy established phonology's theoretical base through phonological oppositions (bilateral, multilateral, privative) and neutralization leading to archiphonemes. Daniel Jones defined the phoneme practically as a 'family of sounds' and created the Cardinal Vowel system and modern IPA usage. Jakobson introduced binary distinctive features (+/-) based on acoustic criteria. Chomsky and Halle's 'The Sound Pattern of English' (1968) introduced Generative Phonology, replacing classical autonomous phonemes with underlying representations transformed by ordered phonological rules into surface phonetic representations.
topics.commonConfusion: Do not confuse phones, phonemes, and allophones. A phone is any actual sound; a phoneme is an abstract mental unit; an allophone is a non-contrastive phonetic variant of a phoneme occurring in complementary distribution or free variation.

topics.title: English Vowels: Monophthongs, Diphthongs, and Triphthongs
topics.coreIdea: Vowels are voiced speech sounds produced with an open vocal tract without airflow obstruction, serving as syllable nuclei. Received Pronunciation (RP) English features 20 vowel phonemes—12 monophthongs (7 short, 5 long) and 8 diphthongs (5 closing, 3 centring)—plus 5 triphthongs formed by glide movements.
topics.vivaAnswer: A vowel is an unobstructed, voiced sound forming the sonorous core of a syllable. English has 12 monophthongs classified by tongue height, tongue frontness, and lip rounding, 8 diphthongs involving a glide between two positions, and 5 triphthongs gliding across three vowel qualities ending in schwa /ə/.
topics.example: /iː/ in 'see' is a long close front unrounded monophthong, /aɪ/ in 'my' is a closing diphthong gliding from open central to front close, and /aɪə/ in 'fire' is a triphthong.
topics.understandMore: Monophthongs remain acoustically stable throughout articulation. The schwa /ə/ is the most frequent English vowel, occurring strictly in unstressed positions as a central, mid, neutral vowel central to rhythm and weak forms. Diphthongs comprise closing types (/eɪ, aɪ, ɔɪ, əʊ, aʊ/) that move toward closer vowels /ɪ/ or /ʊ/, and centring types (/ɪə, eə, ʊə/) gliding toward /ə/ (with /ʊə/ increasingly merged into /ɔː/ in modern RP). Triphthongs (/eɪə, aɪə, ɔɪə, əʊə, aʊə/) represent complex glides within a single syllable, frequently smoothed in rapid speech.
topics.commonConfusion: Students often mistake diphthongs for two separate vowels or syllables; a diphthong is a single phoneme and constitutes one syllable peak. Also, vowel length in English is phonemic (distinguishing words like 'ship' /ʃɪp/ and 'sheep' /ʃiːp/), accompanied by differences in vowel quality and muscular tension (lax vs tense).

topics.title: English Consonants: Voicing, Places, and Manners of Articulation
topics.coreIdea: Consonants are speech sounds produced with partial or complete obstruction of the vocal tract. The 24 English consonants are systematically classified along three phonetic dimensions: state of the glottis (voicing), place of articulation (where the constriction occurs), and manner of articulation (how the airflow is modified).
topics.vivaAnswer: English has 24 consonant phonemes described by voicing (voiced or voiceless), place of articulation (8 places: bilabial, labiodental, dental, alveolar, post-alveolar, palatal, velar, glottal), and manner of articulation (6 manners: plosive, fricative, affricate, nasal, lateral, approximant).
topics.example: /b/ is a voiced bilabial plosive (as in 'bin'), /s/ is a voiceless alveolar fricative ('sun'), and /tʃ/ is a voiceless post-alveolar affricate ('church').
topics.understandMore: Plosives (/p, b, t, d, k, ɡ/) involve complete closure followed by explosive release; fricatives (/f, v, θ, ð, s, z, ʃ, ʒ, h/) involve close approximation producing friction; affricates (/tʃ, dʒ/) begin as plosives and release into fricatives. Nasals (/m, n, ŋ/) have complete oral closure with a lowered velum allowing nasal airflow. The lateral /l/ allows lateral airflow around tongue contact, while approximants (/r, j, w/) involve frictionless narrowing. The sound /w/ is a labial-velar approximant with two simultaneous articulatory places.
topics.commonConfusion: Do not treat /tʃ/ and /dʒ/ as two sequential phonemes; each is a single complex phoneme (affricate). Also distinguish /θ/ (voiceless dental fricative in 'thin') from /ð/ (voiced dental fricative in 'this'), and recognize that /ŋ/ is a velar nasal phoneme, not /n/ + /ɡ/.

topics.title: The Syllable: Phonetic vs. Phonological Definitions, Internal Structure, and Phonotactics
topics.coreIdea: A syllable is a foundational unit of phonological organization consisting of a sonority peak (nucleus) optionally flanked by onsets and codas. Phonetically defined by sonority peaks and phonologically by structural constraints, English syllables exhibit complex phonotactic possibilities permitting onsets up to CCC and codas up to CCCC.
topics.vivaAnswer: Phonetically, a syllable is a sonority peak governed by the Sonority Sequencing Principle. Phonologically, it is a structural unit consisting of an onset and a rhyme, which splits into a nucleus (vowel core) and a coda (final consonants), permitting complex structures up to CCCVCCCC.
topics.example: In the word 'cat' /kæt/, /k/ is the onset, /æ/ is the nucleus, and /t/ is the coda; in 'string' /strɪŋ/, /str/ is a three-consonant onset obeying the phonotactic rule: /s/ + voiceless stop + approximant.
topics.understandMore: The Sonority Hierarchy ranks sounds from vowels > glides > liquids > nasals > fricatives > plosives. In an onset with three consonants, English phonotactics strictly mandates C1 must be /s/, C2 must be /p, t, k/, and C3 must be /l, r, w, j/. Syllables ending in a vowel are open (e.g. 'go' /ɡəʊ/), while those ending in consonants are closed ('cat' /kæt/). Unstressed syllables may lack vowels when a liquid or nasal becomes a syllabic consonant (e.g. /n̩/ in 'button' /ˈbʌtn̩/, /l̩/ in 'bottle' /ˈbɒtl̩/).
topics.commonConfusion: A spoken syllable does not correspond to written orthographic syllable breaks or letter count (e.g., 'cake' has 4 letters but only 1 syllable /keɪk/). Furthermore, English forbids onsets like /ŋ/ or /tl/, illustrating language-specific phonotactic constraints.

topics.title: Strong and Weak Forms, Contractions, Elision, and Assimilation
topics.coreIdea: In connected speech, words undergo systematic phonetic modifications to optimize articulatory ease and rhythm. Function words alternate between citation strong forms and reduced weak forms, while adjacent sounds undergo elision (deletion) or assimilation (regressive, progressive, coalescent), alongside grammatical contractions.
topics.vivaAnswer: Weak forms are the unstressed, reduced pronunciations of grammatical words in connected speech (e.g., 'to' /tə/). Elision is the deletion of sounds (e.g., 'last night' /lɑːs naɪt/), while assimilation is the modification of a sound to match a neighbour (e.g., 'ten boys' /tem bɔɪz/).
topics.example: In 'What do you want?', coalescent assimilation merges /d/ + /j/ into /dʒ/ (/wɒt dʒə wɒnt/), and 'you' appears in its weak form /jə/.
topics.understandMore: Strong forms are reserved for emphasis, contrast, isolation, and phrase-final positions ('Who are you looking for?' /fɔː/). Elision commonly targets alveolar stops /t, d/ in complex consonant clusters ('next day' /neks deɪ/) and weak unstressed vowels ('family' /ˈfæmli/). Assimilation occurs in place (/n/ becomes /m/ before bilabials in 'ten men' /tem men/), voice ('have to' /hæf tə/), or coalescence (/t/ + /j/ → /tʃ/ in 'don't you' /ˈdəʊntʃuː/). Contraction is a conventionalized, orthographically represented shortening ('I am' → 'I'm').
topics.commonConfusion: Weak forms and elision are not 'careless' or 'incorrect' speech; they are the natural phonological rules of English rhythm. Notice also that in elision a sound disappears entirely, whereas in assimilation the sound remains present but transforms.

topics.title: Stress: Definition, Factors of Prominence, Word Stress Rules, and Sentence Stress
topics.coreIdea: Stress is the relative auditory prominence given to a syllable, produced by heightened articulatory energy. Governed primarily by pitch change alongside loudness, length, and vowel quality, stress operates at word level (lexical stress patterns and noun-verb shifts) and sentence level (stress-timing and information focus).
topics.vivaAnswer: Stress is syllable prominence perceived through four acoustic factors: pitch change (most important), loudness, length/duration, and full vowel quality. In English words, stress distinguishes nouns from verbs (e.g., ˈrecord vs reˈcord) and establishes stress-timed sentence rhythm.
topics.example: In the noun-verb pair 'present', the noun is stressed on the first syllable (ˈpresent /ˈpreznt/) while the verb is stressed on the second (preˈsent /prɪˈzent/).
topics.understandMore: Stress levels include primary (ˈ), secondary (ˌ), and unstressed. Rules for polysyllabic words include suffix-determined stress (penultimate stress before -tion, -ic, -ity; antepenultimate before -ate, -ize; final on -ee, -eer). Compound nouns stress the first element (ˈblackbird), whereas compound adjectives and verbs stress the second (bad-ˈtempered, underˈstand). In sentences, content words (nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs) receive stress, while function words remain unstressed unless highlighted by contrastive or emphatic stress.
topics.commonConfusion: Loudness alone does not create stress; psychoacoustic research proves pitch movement is the most potent perceptual cue. Additionally, English is a stress-timed language where intervals between stressed syllables are roughly equal, unlike syllable-timed languages where every syllable has equal duration.

topics.title: Chunking, Tone, and Tone Units
topics.coreIdea: Chunking divides continuous spoken discourse into manageable tone units or thought groups, each anchored by a prominent pitch movement (tone). The tone unit is the fundamental building block of spoken prosody, possessing a hierarchical structure centered on the obligatory tonic syllable.
topics.vivaAnswer: Chunking is dividing continuous speech into meaningful tone units (thought groups) separated by pauses. A tone unit has an obligatory tonic syllable (nucleus) carrying the primary pitch movement (tone), flanked optionally by a pre-head, head, and tail.
topics.example: In the utterance | She ˈbought a ↘CAR |, 'car' is the tonic syllable bearing the falling pitch movement, preceded by the head 'ˈbought a' and pre-head 'She'.
topics.understandMore: Natural chunking respects grammatical and sense boundaries (clauses, phrases) and respiration needs. Pitch movement on the tonic syllable constitutes tone: falling (certainty/finality), rising (incompleteness/question), fall-rise (reservation/doubt), rise-fall (strong surprise/sarcasm), and level (routine/boredom). In tone unit structure, the tonic syllable is the only mandatory element; pre-head covers unstressed syllables before the head, head runs from the first stressed syllable to the tonic, and tail includes any syllables following the tonic.
topics.commonConfusion: Do not confuse tone in intonation languages with lexical tone in tonal languages (like Mandarin). In English, tone operates at the phrase/utterance level to signal pragmatic meaning, not to change individual lexical word definitions. Furthermore, a tone unit does not necessarily equal a syntactic sentence.

topics.title: Intonation: Definition, Four Functions, and Pitch Contours
topics.coreIdea: Intonation is the meaningful variation of pitch across entire utterances. It fulfills four core communicative functions—grammatical, attitudinal, discourse, and accentual—allowing speakers to signal sentence types, emotional attitudes, conversational management, and information focus.
topics.vivaAnswer: Intonation is the melody of speech formed by pitch variation across utterances. It serves four key functions: grammatical (distinguishing questions from statements), attitudinal (expressing emotion and attitude), discourse (managing turn-taking and given vs new information), and accentual (focusing the tonic syllable).
topics.example: The tag question 'It's cold, isn't it?' means 'I expect you to agree' with a falling tag (↘), but becomes a genuine question with a rising tag (↗).
topics.understandMore: Falling intonation (↘) is standard for declarative statements, wh-questions, commands, exclamations, and final items in lists. Rising intonation (↗) characterizes yes/no questions, polite requests, encouragement, and open/listing items. Fall-rise intonation (↘↗) conveys reservation, partial agreement ('It's ↘↗nice...'), polite dissent, and contrast. Rise-fall (↗↘) signals strong emotion, surprise ('That's ↗↘amazing!'), or irony. Intonational meaning interacts directly with pragmatics and speech acts.
topics.commonConfusion: Rising intonation does not automatically mean 'question'; wh-questions routinely use falling intonation, while rising intonation can indicate polite listing or unfinished statements. Tone is the pitch change on a single syllable, while intonation is the overarching pitch pattern across an entire utterance.

topics.title: IPA Transcription of Connected Speech and Linking Phenomena
topics.coreIdea: Connected speech transcription represents natural spoken language using standard IPA notation, capturing systematic alterations from citation forms. It accounts for weak forms, elisions, assimilations, and linking phenomena (linking /r/, intrusive /r/, and glide insertion /j, w/).
topics.vivaAnswer: IPA transcription of connected speech captures fluent speech modifications using broad phonemic notation / / annotated for weak forms, elisions, assimilations, stress marks, and linking phenomena such as linking /r/, intrusive /r/, and glide insertions (/j/, /w/).
topics.example: The sentence 'I want to go to the shop' changes from citation /aɪ wɒnt tuː ɡəʊ tuː ðiː ʃɒp/ to connected speech /aɪ wɒnə ɡəʊ tə ðə ʃɒp/ through /t/-elision and vowel reductions to schwa.
topics.understandMore: Broad transcription represents contrastive phonemes between slashes / /, while narrow transcription adds diacritics in square brackets [ ] to indicate phonetic detail (aspiration, nasalization, syllabicity). In non-rhotic accents like RP, linking /r/ reintroduces silent orthographic 'r' before following vowels ('far away' /fɑːrəweɪ/), while intrusive /r/ inserts /r/ after /ɔː, ɑː, ə/ where no orthographic 'r' exists ('law and order' /lɔːrənd ɔːdə/). Vowel-vowel transitions insert /j/ after front vowels ('he asked' /hiːjɑːskt/) and /w/ after back rounded vowels ('go away' /ɡəʊwəweɪ/).
topics.commonConfusion: Connected speech is not 'sloppy' or substandard speech; it is rule-governed, systematic phonological behavior characteristic of all native speakers. Pronouncing every word in its isolated citation form sounds artificial and hinders natural stress-timed English rhythm.

questions.question: What is phonetics?
questions.directAnswer: Phonetics is the scientific study of the physical properties of human speech sounds.
questions.vivaAnswer: Phonetics is the branch of linguistics that studies the physical properties of speech sounds. It investigates how sounds are produced by the vocal organs, transmitted as sound waves through the air, and perceived by the human ear, regardless of language meaning.
keyPoints: Scientific study of speech sounds as physical events
Covers production, transmission, and perception
Universal across all human languages
Transcribed using square brackets [ ]
questions.explanation: Phonetics treats speech sounds as concrete acoustic and biological events. For example, when saying 'pin', phonetics details the muscular movement of the lips, vocal fold vibration, and sound wave frequencies of [pʰ], [ɪ], and [n], without considering whether the sounds contrast words in English.

questions.question: What is phonology?
questions.directAnswer: Phonology is the study of how speech sounds function and pattern within a specific language system.
questions.vivaAnswer: Phonology is the branch of linguistics that studies how speech sounds function, pattern, and organize within a particular language. It focuses on abstract mental sound units called phonemes and the sound contrasts that distinguish word meaning.
keyPoints: Study of sound systems and patterns in a language
Deals with abstract, mental sound representations
Focuses on contrastive, meaning-distinguishing units (phonemes)
Transcribed using slashes / /
questions.explanation: Unlike phonetics which is universal and purely physical, phonology is language-specific. It asks which sound differences create distinctions in meaning (such as /p/ vs /b/ in English 'pin' vs 'bin') and what rules govern sound combinations (phonotactics).

questions.question: What are the fundamental differences between phonetics and phonology?
questions.directAnswer: Phonetics is universal, concrete, and physical (studying phones in [ ]), whereas phonology is language-specific, mental, and functional (studying phonemes in / /).
questions.vivaAnswer: The main difference is that phonetics studies the physical, universal properties of all speech sounds (production, acoustic transmission, perception), while phonology studies how sounds function and contrast within a specific language's mental system. Phonetics uses square brackets [ ] for phones, whereas phonology uses slashes / / for phonemes.
keyPoints: Physical/concrete (phonetics) vs. abstract/mental (phonology)
Universal (all human speech) vs. language-specific
Does not consider meaning vs. focuses on meaning distinction
Phone [ ] vs. phoneme / /
questions.explanation: A clear example is aspiration in English: [pʰ] in 'pin' and [p] in 'spin' are phonetically two distinct sounds because [pʰ] has a puff of air. Phonologically, however, both represent the single phoneme /p/ in English because swapping them does not change word meaning.

questions.question: What are the three main branches of phonetics?
questions.directAnswer: The three main branches are articulatory phonetics, acoustic phonetics, and auditory phonetics.
questions.vivaAnswer: Phonetics is divided into three branches based on the speech communication chain: articulatory phonetics (how sounds are produced by the vocal organs), acoustic phonetics (how sound waves travel through the air), and auditory phonetics (how sounds are received and perceived by the ear and brain).
keyPoints: Articulatory phonetics: sound production (speaker)
Acoustic phonetics: sound wave transmission (medium)
Auditory phonetics: sound perception (listener)
questions.explanation: These three branches correspond to the speaker's mouth, the transmitting air, and the listener's ear. In linguistics viva examinations, articulatory phonetics is the most frequently tested branch.

questions.question: What does articulatory phonetics study, and what are its key parameters?
questions.directAnswer: Articulatory phonetics studies how speech sounds are produced by the vocal organs using parameters like voicing, place of articulation, and manner of articulation.
questions.vivaAnswer: Articulatory phonetics examines how speech sounds are produced by the human vocal organs, including the lungs, vocal cords, tongue, lips, teeth, and palate. It classifies sounds primarily through three parameters: the state of the glottis (voicing), the place of articulation (where constriction occurs), and the manner of articulation (how airflow is modified).
keyPoints: Focuses on speech production by vocal organs
Key articulators: lips, teeth, alveolar ridge, palate, velum, vocal cords
Primary descriptive triad: voicing, place, manner
Example: /b/ is described as a voiced bilabial plosive
questions.explanation: Articulatory descriptions provide anatomical precision. For instance, in producing /t/, the tongue blade contacts the alveolar ridge, completely obstructing the airstream before releasing it without vocal cord vibration (voiceless alveolar plosive).

questions.question: What is acoustic phonetics and what physical properties does it measure?
questions.directAnswer: Acoustic phonetics studies speech sound waves traveling through the air, measuring frequency, amplitude, and duration.
questions.vivaAnswer: Acoustic phonetics analyzes the physical properties of speech sound waves as they travel between speaker and listener. It measures three primary properties: frequency (pitch), amplitude (loudness/intensity), and duration (length), typically utilizing instruments such as sound spectrographs to produce spectrograms.
keyPoints: Analyzes sound waves in the transmission phase
Measures frequency (Hertz), amplitude (decibels), and duration (milliseconds)
Key concepts: fundamental frequency (F0), harmonics, formants (F1, F2)
Instrument: Spectrogram
questions.explanation: Acoustic phonetics is crucial for identifying vowel qualities by measuring formant frequencies (F1 corresponds inversely to tongue height; F2 corresponds to tongue frontness). It bridges articulatory movements and auditory perception.

questions.question: What is auditory phonetics and how does it differ from acoustic phonetics?
questions.directAnswer: Acoustic phonetics examines the physical sound wave in the air, while auditory phonetics examines how that sound wave is detected by the ear and interpreted by the brain.
questions.vivaAnswer: Auditory (or perceptual) phonetics investigates how speech signals are received, converted into neural impulses by the ear, and processed psychoacoustically by the listener's brain. In contrast, acoustic phonetics measures the objective physical wave itself (frequency and amplitude) before it enters the human auditory system.
keyPoints: Acoustic: objective physical wave properties (spectrograms, waveforms)
Auditory: subjective psychoacoustic hearing and perceptual discrimination
Anatomical focus: cochlea, eardrum, auditory nerve, and auditory cortex
questions.explanation: While acoustic instruments measure absolute decibels and Hertz, auditory phonetics studies perceived loudness, pitch contours, and how humans categorize continuous acoustic signals into discrete phonemic categories.

questions.question: How do phonetics and phonology correlate and depend on each other?
questions.directAnswer: Phonetics provides the empirical raw material of speech sounds, while phonology provides the structural rules and functional organization of those sounds.
questions.vivaAnswer: Phonetics and phonology are mutually dependent. Phonetics provides the empirical raw data—the physical sounds that the vocal organs produce—while phonology organizes that data into functional, meaningful linguistic patterns. You cannot describe phonological systems without phonetic data, nor can you understand linguistic communication with phonetics alone.
keyPoints: Phonetics provides raw physical sounds; phonology organizes them
Phonology selects a subset of phonetic possibilities to create meaning contrasts
They share the same subject matter (speech sounds) at different analytical levels
Phonetics is concrete; phonology is abstract
questions.explanation: In English, [p] and [pʰ] are phonetically distinct in airflow, but phonology reveals that this difference is predictable and non-contrastive. In languages like Hindi or Thai, however, this very phonetic difference is phonological, distinguishing entirely different words.

questions.question: Why are square brackets [ ] used for phonetic transcription and slashes / / for phonological transcription?
questions.directAnswer: Square brackets [ ] enclose concrete phones (actual sounds), while slashes / / enclose abstract phonemes (meaning-distinguishing units).
questions.vivaAnswer: Square brackets [ ] represent phonetic transcription, indicating actual, physical sounds (phones) with exact acoustic and articulatory details, such as aspiration [pʰ]. Slashes / / represent phonemic transcription, indicating abstract, functional sound units (phonemes) stored in the speaker's mental lexicon, such as /p/.
keyPoints: [ ] = phonetic (phones, allophones, narrow details)
/ / = phonemic (phonemes, broad contrastive units)
Confusing the two brackets is a serious theoretical error in viva
questions.explanation: Transcribing /pʰ/ is incorrect because aspiration is not contrastive in English; the phonemic unit is /p/, while its physical phonetic realization in 'pin' is written [pʰ].

questions.question: Why is phonetics considered universal while phonology is language-specific?
questions.directAnswer: Phonetics applies universally to human anatomy and physics, whereas phonology describes the unique sound rules and contrasts chosen by a specific language.
questions.vivaAnswer: Phonetics is universal because all humans share the same vocal apparatus and physical acoustics; any human vocal tract can potentially produce an alveolar click or a nasal vowel. Phonology is language-specific because each individual language selects only a small subset of sounds and establishes its own unique rules for which sounds contrast meaning.
keyPoints: Phonetics is universal: biological vocal anatomy and physical acoustics
Phonology is language-specific: arbitrary, culturally inherited sound systems
The same phone can be an allophone in Language A and a phoneme in Language B
questions.explanation: For example, aspiration ([p] vs [pʰ]) exists phonetically in both English and Hindi. In English, it is non-contrastive (allophonic), but in Hindi, it is phonological, differentiating 'pal' (moment) from 'phal' (fruit).

questions.question: What is a phoneme?
questions.directAnswer: A phoneme is the smallest abstract contrastive sound unit in a language that can distinguish one word from another.
questions.vivaAnswer: A phoneme is the smallest contrastive unit of sound in a language that is capable of distinguishing word meaning. It is an abstract, mental representation in the speaker's mind, written between slashes / /, and proven by minimal pairs like /p/ and /b/ in 'pat' and 'bat'.
keyPoints: Smallest meaning-distinguishing sound unit
Abstract mental representation, not a physical sound
Enclosed in slashes / /
Established using minimal pairs
questions.explanation: English has approximately 44 phonemes. A phoneme does not possess inherent semantic meaning of its own, but altering a single phoneme alters the word's meaning entirely (e.g. /kæt/ 'cat' vs /mæt/ 'mat').

questions.question: What is a phone?
questions.directAnswer: A phone is any actual, physical speech sound produced by a human speaker, written in square brackets [ ].
questions.vivaAnswer: A phone is a concrete, physical sound event produced by the vocal tract and capable of being heard, recorded, and acoustically measured. Unlike phonemes, phones are not abstract and are transcribed within square brackets [ ].
keyPoints: Concrete, measurable physical speech sound
Enclosed in square brackets [ ]
Unlimited in variation across speakers and contexts
The physical realization of an underlying phoneme
questions.explanation: Phones are the objective phonetic events of speech. For instance, the aspirated sound [pʰ] in 'pin' and the unaspirated sound [p] in 'spin' are two physically distinct phones.

questions.question: What is an allophone?
questions.directAnswer: An allophone is a predictable phonetic variant of a phoneme that does not change the meaning of a word.
questions.vivaAnswer: An allophone is a contextual phonetic variant of a single phoneme. When a phoneme is realized as different physical sounds in different phonetic environments without changing the word's meaning, those variant sounds are called allophones of that phoneme.
keyPoints: Positional or contextual variant of a phoneme
Does not create a contrast in meaning
Usually occurs in complementary distribution or free variation
Transcribed in square brackets [ ]
questions.explanation: In English, the phoneme /l/ has two major allophones: clear [l] before vowels ('light') and dark (velarized) [ɫ] after vowels or word-finally ('ball'). English speakers recognize them as the same functional sound.

questions.question: How do you distinguish between a phone, a phoneme, and an allophone?
questions.directAnswer: A phone is any real sound [ ]; a phoneme is an abstract contrastive category / /; an allophone is a specific physical member belonging to a phoneme family.
questions.vivaAnswer: A phone is any concrete sound produced by the vocal organs, transcribed in [ ]. A phoneme is an abstract, meaning-distinguishing sound unit stored in the mind, transcribed in / /. An allophone is a specific phonetic variant of a phoneme occurring in predictable environments that does not alter meaning.
keyPoints: Phone: concrete, universal physical sound [p]
Phoneme: abstract, language-specific mental category /p/
Allophone: sub-member variant of a phoneme ([pʰ], [p])
Every allophone is a phone, but phones only become allophones relative to a specific phoneme
questions.explanation: An analogy is a family: the phoneme is the family surname (abstract concept /p/), while allophones are the individual family members ([pʰ], [p], [p̚]), and any human being is a phone.

questions.question: What is a minimal pair and what is its role in phonology?
questions.directAnswer: A minimal pair is a pair of words that differ by only one sound in the same position, proving that the two sounds are distinct phonemes.
questions.vivaAnswer: A minimal pair consists of two words in a language that differ in meaning and are identical in pronunciation except for a single sound segment in the same phonetic position. Because the substitution of one sound for another changes word meaning, minimal pairs prove that the two sounds are separate phonemes.
keyPoints: Two words differing by exactly one sound in identical position
Must result in a difference in word meaning
Primary methodological tool for establishing phonemic inventory
Examples: 'pat' /pæt/ vs 'bat' /bæt/, 'ship' /ʃɪp/ vs 'sheep' /ʃiːp/
questions.explanation: In 'sip' /sɪp/ and 'zip' /zɪp/, the only phonetic difference is the initial consonant (/s/ vs /z/). Because 'sip' and 'zip' mean different things, /s/ and /z/ are established as distinct phonemes in English.

questions.question: Distinguish between complementary distribution and free variation.
questions.directAnswer: Complementary distribution means sounds occur in mutually exclusive environments, while free variation means sounds can substitute for each other in the same environment without changing meaning.
questions.vivaAnswer: Complementary distribution occurs when two phonetic variants never appear in the same phonetic environment; where one occurs, the other cannot. Free variation occurs when two different phones can appear in the exact same position without altering the word's meaning and without being determined by phonetic environment.
keyPoints: Complementary distribution: mutually exclusive environments (e.g., [pʰ] syllable-initially, [p] after /s/)
Complementary distribution is the hallmark of allophony
Free variation: interchangeable in the same environment (e.g., released [p] vs unreleased [p̚] in 'stop')
Neither phenomenon causes a change in lexical meaning
questions.explanation: Like Superman and Clark Kent, allophones in complementary distribution are never seen in the same place at the same time. In contrast, free variation represents optional stylistic or dialectal freedom.

questions.question: Who was Nikolai Trubetzkoy and what was his major contribution to phonology?
questions.directAnswer: Nikolai Trubetzkoy was a founder of the Prague School who established phonology as a separate discipline defined by distinctive sound oppositions.
questions.vivaAnswer: Nikolai Trubetzkoy (1890–1938) was a Russian linguist and central figure in the Prague Linguistic Circle. In his seminal 1939 work 'Grundzüge der Phonologie' (Principles of Phonology), he clearly separated phonology from phonetics, defining the phoneme by its distinctive, meaning-differentiating function within a system of phonological oppositions.
keyPoints: Prague School founder; author of 'Grundzüge der Phonologie' (1939)
Separated phonetics (physical) from phonology (functional)
Defined phonemes through their distinctive function
Introduced theories of phonological oppositions, neutralization, and markedness
questions.explanation: Trubetzkoy shifted linguistic inquiry from the physical description of sound substance to the functional relational network among sounds. His structural framework remains foundational to modern phonological theory.

questions.question: Explain Trubetzkoy's concepts of phonological oppositions and neutralization.
questions.directAnswer: Phonological oppositions are contrastive sound relationships (e.g. privative), while neutralization occurs when an opposition is cancelled in specific positions, yielding an archiphoneme.
questions.vivaAnswer: Trubetzkoy classified phonological contrasts into oppositions, such as privative oppositions where one member has a feature and the other lacks it (e.g. voiced /b/ vs voiceless /p/). Neutralization occurs when an opposition is cancelled in a specific environment; for instance, in German, the voicing contrast between /t/ and /d/ is neutralized word-finally to [t], represented as the archiphoneme /T/.
keyPoints: Oppositions: bilateral/multilateral, proportional/isolated, privative/gradual/equipollent
Privative opposition: presence vs absence of a mark (e.g. [±voice])
Neutralization: loss of contrastive power in specific phonotactic positions
Archiphoneme: abstract unit representing the neutralized opposition
questions.explanation: In German 'Rad' (wheel) and 'Rat' (advice), both end with [t] on the surface due to word-final devoicing neutralization. Trubetzkoy also developed the theory of markedness, where one member is unmarked (default) and the other is marked.

questions.question: What was Roman Jakobson's Distinctive Feature Theory?
questions.directAnswer: Jakobson proposed that phonemes are not indivisible units but bundles of universal, binary (+/-) acoustic features.
questions.vivaAnswer: Roman Jakobson (1896–1982), associated with the Prague School and later Harvard/MIT, introduced Distinctive Feature Theory. He demonstrated that the phoneme is not the ultimate minimal unit of language, but rather a bundle of smaller, simultaneous binary (+ or −) distinctive features based primarily on acoustic properties (such as [±voice], [±nasal], [±grave]).
keyPoints: Phonemes decomposed into bundles of concurrent features
Binary values (+/-) represent presence or absence of a feature
Features are universal across all human languages
Initially based on acoustic/spectrographic criteria rather than articulatory ones
questions.explanation: Under Jakobson's theory, /p/ and /b/ are identical in every feature except that /b/ is [+voiced] while /p/ is [−voiced]. This insight made phonology compositional and paved the way for modern generative phonology.

questions.question: How did Daniel Jones define the phoneme as a 'family of sounds'?
questions.directAnswer: Daniel Jones defined the phoneme practically as a family of phonetically related sounds that never occur in the same context in a given language.
questions.vivaAnswer: Daniel Jones (1881–1967), the leading British phonetician, took a practical, physical approach to the phoneme. He famously defined it as 'a family of sounds in a given language which are related in character and are used in such a way that no one member ever occurs in a word in the same phonetic context as any other member.'
keyPoints: Physical and concrete view of the phoneme (British phonetic tradition)
Defined phoneme as a 'family of sounds' (allophones)
Emphasized phonetic similarity and complementary distribution
Contrasted with the purely abstract functionalist Prague School view
questions.explanation: Jones's definition grounded phonology in empirical articulatory realities. For Jones, the phoneme was an inventory of related physical phones grouped by strict distribution rather than an unobservable mental entity.

questions.question: What is Daniel Jones's Cardinal Vowel system and why is it important?
questions.directAnswer: The Cardinal Vowel system is a set of 16 reference vowels (8 primary, 8 secondary) based on physiological tongue extremes to map any vowel sound.
questions.vivaAnswer: Daniel Jones developed the Cardinal Vowel system as a set of objective, standardized reference points for identifying and describing vowels in any language. Based on the physiological limits of tongue height (close vs open) and frontness (front vs back), it consists of 8 primary and 8 secondary cardinal vowels, providing the foundation for the IPA vowel quadrilateral.
keyPoints: Invented by Daniel Jones at University College London
Set of 8 primary and 8 secondary fixed reference vowels
Based on extreme physiological positions of the tongue and lip postures
Serves as the universal mapping framework for the IPA vowel chart
questions.explanation: Cardinal vowels are theoretical yardsticks rather than sounds of a specific language (though Cardinal 1 [i] is close to French 'si'). In viva, Jones is also celebrated for his English Pronouncing Dictionary (EPD) and the codification of RP.

questions.question: What was Chomsky and Halle's critique of the classical autonomous phoneme in Generative Phonology?
questions.directAnswer: Chomsky and Halle criticized the classical phoneme as an unnecessary artificial level that obscures overarching morphological and phonological generalizations.
questions.vivaAnswer: In 'The Sound Pattern of English' (SPE, 1968), Noam Chomsky and Morris Halle argued against the classical structuralist phoneme (as used by Jones and Trubetzkoy). They criticized the autonomous phonemic level for imposing strict biuniqueness and surface invariance conditions, which prevented linguists from expressing unified phonological processes across morpheme boundaries; instead, they replaced it with underlying systematic phonemic representations mapped directly to surface phonetic forms via ordered rules.
keyPoints: Rejection of classical autonomous phoneme and biuniqueness constraint
Structuralist phonemics misses significant phonological generalizations across word boundaries
Replaced with systematic phonemic level (Underlying Representation)
Chomsky & Halle SPE (1968) introduced Generative Phonology
questions.explanation: For example, in Russian voicing assimilation, treating the phoneme as an autonomous invariant forces two completely different mechanisms for the same physical voicing process. Generative phonology eliminates this redundancy.

questions.question: Explain the generative phonological model: Underlying representation -> Phonological rules -> Surface representation.
questions.directAnswer: Underlying representation is the abstract mental form stored in memory; phonological rules modify it contextually to generate the surface spoken form.
questions.vivaAnswer: In generative phonology, the Underlying Representation (UR) is the abstract mental form stored in the speaker's lexicon, coded in distinctive features. Ordered phonological rules then apply to this form depending on morphological and phonetic environment. The final output is the Surface Representation (SR), which represents the actual physical pronunciation.
keyPoints: Underlying Representation (UR): abstract, stored in mental lexicon (e.g. /kæt + z/)
Phonological Rules: formal rewrite statements (A → B / C __ D)
Surface Representation (SR): actual phonetic realization (e.g. [kæts] due to voicing assimilation)
Connects phonology with morphology and psychological grammar
questions.explanation: For example, the underlying plural morpheme /-z/ is modified by a rule: 'Voiced fricative becomes voiceless after a voiceless consonant' (/z/ → [s] / [-voice] __), converting /kæt + z/ into surface [kæts].

questions.question: How does the phoneme-allophone relationship in phonology connect to morphemes and allomorphs in morphology (E411)?
questions.directAnswer: The phoneme-allophone relationship is structurally parallel to the morpheme-allomorph relationship: an abstract mental unit realized as predictable contextual variants.
questions.vivaAnswer: The relationship between a phoneme and its allophones directly parallels the morphological relationship between a morpheme and its allomorphs. Just as an abstract phoneme /p/ has contextual phonetic realizations ([pʰ] in 'pin', [p] in 'spin'), an abstract morpheme (like the English plural {-s}) has phonologically conditioned allomorphic realizations: [s] in 'cats', [z] in 'dogs', and [ɪz] in 'busses'.
keyPoints: Structural isomorphism between phonology and morphology
Phoneme : Allophone = Morpheme : Allomorph
Abstract mental invariant vs. contextually conditioned realization
Governed by morphophonological rules
questions.explanation: This connection represents the subfield of Morphophonology in E411. In both cases, the variants are in complementary distribution determined by surrounding phonetic environments.

questions.question: What is a vowel sound from an articulatory and phonological perspective?
questions.directAnswer: A vowel is a voiced speech sound produced without any obstruction of airflow in the vocal tract, functioning as the nucleus of a syllable.
questions.vivaAnswer: Articulatively, a vowel is a speech sound produced when the airstream escapes continuously from the lungs through the pharynx and mouth without any obstruction, blockage, or audible friction. Phonologically, vowels are voiced sounds that occupy the central, most sonorous peak (the nucleus) of every syllable.
keyPoints: No obstruction or friction in the vocal tract
Always voiced in English
Forms the indispensable nucleus (peak) of a syllable
Classified by tongue position and lip posture
questions.explanation: If air is obstructed, the sound becomes a consonant. In English, you cannot have a well-formed syllable without a vowel (or a vowel substitute like a syllabic consonant).

questions.question: What are the three main articulatory criteria used to describe and classify vowels?
questions.directAnswer: Vowels are classified by tongue height (vertical), tongue frontness (horizontal), and lip rounding (shape).
questions.vivaAnswer: Vowels are classified based on three primary articulatory dimensions: tongue height (close/high, mid, or open/low), tongue position or frontness (front, central, or back), and lip shape (rounded, spread, or neutral). A fourth secondary factor is length or muscular tension (long/tense vs short/lax).
keyPoints: Tongue height: close (high), close-mid, open-mid, open (low)
Tongue frontness: front, central, back
Lip shape: rounded, spread, unrounded/neutral
Length/tension: long vs short (lax)
questions.explanation: For example, /iː/ (as in 'see') is described as a close front spread long vowel, while /uː/ ('food') is a close back rounded long vowel.

questions.question: What is a monophthong and how many monophthongs are there in RP English?
questions.directAnswer: A monophthong is a pure, single vowel sound where the vocal organs remain steady, with 12 monophthongs in RP English.
questions.vivaAnswer: A monophthong (also called a pure vowel) is a vowel produced with the tongue and lips remaining in a constant, fixed position throughout its articulation without any audible glide. Received Pronunciation (RP) English has exactly 12 monophthong phonemes, divided into 7 short vowels and 5 long vowels.
keyPoints: Pure vowel: steady-state acoustic quality throughout production
No gliding movement of the tongue or lips
12 monophthongs in RP English: 7 short and 5 long
Examples: /iː, ɪ, e, æ, ɑː, ɒ, ɔː, ʊ, uː, ʌ, ɜː, ə/
questions.explanation: Monophthongs contrast with diphthongs, which involve a smooth movement from one articulatory posture to another within the same syllable.

questions.question: Distinguish between short and long vowels in English with IPA examples.
questions.directAnswer: English has 5 long vowels (indicated with a length mark ː) and 7 short vowels, differing in duration, tension, and vowel quality.
questions.vivaAnswer: English has 5 long vowels (/iː, ɑː, ɔː, uː, ɜː/), written with a length mark ː, which are phonetically longer and tenser, and 7 short vowels (/ɪ, e, æ, ɒ, ʊ, ʌ, ə/), which are shorter, laxer, and produced with less muscular tension. They are contrastive phonemes that differentiate words like 'ship' /ʃɪp/ and 'sheep' /ʃiːp/.
keyPoints: 5 Long vowels: /iː/ (see), /ɑː/ (car), /ɔː/ (saw), /uː/ (food), /ɜː/ (bird)
7 Short vowels: /ɪ/ (sit), /e/ (bed), /æ/ (cat), /ɒ/ (hot), /ʊ/ (put), /ʌ/ (cup), /ə/ (about)
Phonetic differences: duration, vowel tract quality/position, and muscle tension (tense vs lax)
Phonemic contrast proven by minimal pairs (e.g. /fʊl/ 'full' vs /fuːl/ 'fool')
questions.explanation: Long vowels are not merely longer versions of short vowels; their articulatory positions differ. For example, /iː/ is higher and fronter than /ɪ/.

questions.question: What is the schwa /ə/ and why is it unique in English phonology?
questions.directAnswer: The schwa /ə/ is the most frequent English vowel: a central, mid, neutral vowel that occurs exclusively in unstressed syllables.
questions.vivaAnswer: The schwa /ə/ is the most common vowel sound in the English language. It is a mid-central neutral vowel produced with the vocal tract in a completely relaxed resting position. Its defining phonological property is that it occurs strictly in unstressed syllables, forming the foundation of weak forms and English stress-timed rhythm.
keyPoints: Most frequent vowel in spoken English
Articulatory status: mid, central, neutral lip posture
Restricted distribution: occurs ONLY in unstressed syllables
Crucial for weak forms (e.g. 'to' /tə/, 'the' /ðə/) and connected speech rhythm
questions.explanation: Examples include the initial syllable of 'about' /əˈbaʊt/ and the final syllable of 'teacher' /ˈtiːtʃə/. A stressed schwa does not exist in English phonology.

questions.question: What is a diphthong and how many are there in RP English?
questions.directAnswer: A diphthong is a single syllable vowel sound that glides smoothly from one vowel quality to another, with 8 diphthongs in RP.
questions.vivaAnswer: A diphthong is a complex vowel sound where the vocal organs glide continuously from one vowel position to another within a single syllable. Received Pronunciation English contains 8 diphthong phonemes, subdivided into closing diphthongs (gliding toward /ɪ/ or /ʊ/) and centring diphthongs (gliding toward /ə/).
keyPoints: Gliding vowel: moves from initial position to target position within one syllable
Functions as a single phonemic nucleus
8 diphthongs in RP English
Subdivided into closing (5) and centring (3)
questions.explanation: The first element of an English diphthong is longer and stronger (prominent) than the second gliding element. For example, in /aɪ/ ('my'), most duration is spent on the open central starting quality.

questions.question: What is the difference between closing diphthongs and centring diphthongs?
questions.directAnswer: Closing diphthongs glide upward toward a close vowel (/ɪ/ or /ʊ/), whereas centring diphthongs glide inward toward the central schwa /ə/.
questions.vivaAnswer: Closing diphthongs involve an upward movement of the tongue toward a higher, closer vowel position (either front /ɪ/ or back /ʊ/), causing the jaw to close. In contrast, centring diphthongs glide from peripheral vowel positions inward toward the central, neutral vowel schwa /ə/.
keyPoints: Closing diphthongs (5): glide toward /ɪ/ or /ʊ/ (jaw closes)
Centring diphthongs (3): glide toward central schwa /ə/
Closing subgroups: ending in /ɪ/ (/eɪ, aɪ, ɔɪ/) and ending in /ʊ/ (/əʊ, aʊ/)
Centring group: /ɪə, eə, ʊə/
questions.explanation: Closing diphthongs end in high vowels with reduced mouth opening, while centring diphthongs relax the vocal tract toward the mid-central rest position.

questions.question: Name the 5 closing diphthongs in RP English with example words.
questions.directAnswer: The 5 closing diphthongs are /eɪ/ (say), /aɪ/ (my), /ɔɪ/ (boy), /əʊ/ (go), and /aʊ/ (now).
questions.vivaAnswer: The 5 closing diphthongs in RP English are divided into two sets: three gliding toward /ɪ/—/eɪ/ (as in 'say', 'make'), /aɪ/ (as in 'my', 'time'), and /ɔɪ/ (as in 'boy', 'coin'); and two gliding toward /ʊ/—/əʊ/ (as in 'go', 'home') and /aʊ/ (as in 'how', 'now').
keyPoints: Gliding to /ɪ/: /eɪ/ (face, day), /aɪ/ (price, fly), /ɔɪ/ (choice, toy)
Gliding to /ʊ/: /əʊ/ (goat, show), /aʊ/ (mouth, loud)
All involve jaw movement toward closer tongue height
questions.explanation: In older British transcriptions, /əʊ/ was written as /oʊ/, but modern RP initiates the glide from a central schwa-like quality [ə], moving toward [ʊ].

questions.question: Name the 3 centring diphthongs in RP English and explain the modern status of /ʊə/.
questions.directAnswer: The 3 centring diphthongs are /ɪə/ (near), /eə/ (hair), and /ʊə/ (tour), with /ʊə/ rapidly merging into /ɔː/ in modern RP.
questions.vivaAnswer: The 3 centring diphthongs in RP English are /ɪə/ (as in 'ear', 'here'), /eə/ (as in 'air', 'care'), and /ʊə/ (as in 'tour', 'pure'). In contemporary British English, /ʊə/ is increasingly rare and is undergoing a phonemic merger with the long monophthong /ɔː/, so words like 'sure' and 'tour' are frequently pronounced /ʃɔː/ and /tɔː/.
keyPoints: /ɪə/: front close to central ('near', 'idea')
/eə/: front mid to central ('square', 'where')
/ʊə/: back close to central ('cure', 'tour')
Sociolinguistic trend: /ʊə/ merging into /ɔː/ (diphthong leveling)
questions.explanation: This change is an active phonological shift in modern British English. Examiners often award high marks for mentioning this merger in viva.

questions.question: What is a triphthong and how is it formed in English?
questions.directAnswer: A triphthong is a glide across three vowel qualities within a single syllable, formed by adding schwa /ə/ to a closing diphthong.
questions.vivaAnswer: A triphthong is the most complex English vowel sound, consisting of a continuous glide through three distinct vowel qualities within a single syllable. In English, triphthongs are formed by attaching the central schwa /ə/ onto the end of the five closing diphthongs.
keyPoints: Continuous glide through three vowel qualities in one syllable
Formed by closing diphthong + /ə/
5 triphthongs in English
Frequently undergo 'smoothing' (monophthongization) in rapid connected speech
questions.explanation: When the suffix '-er' or '-a' is added to a closing diphthong, or within a single morpheme like 'fire' /faɪə/, a triphthong is articulated.

questions.question: List the 5 English triphthongs with example words.
questions.directAnswer: The 5 English triphthongs are /eɪə/ (player), /aɪə/ (fire), /ɔɪə/ (loyal), /əʊə/ (lower), and /aʊə/ (power).
questions.vivaAnswer: The 5 triphthongs in English are: /eɪə/ (from /eɪ/ + /ə/, e.g., 'player', 'layer'), /aɪə/ (from /aɪ/ + /ə/, e.g., 'fire', 'tyre'), /ɔɪə/ (from /ɔɪ/ + /ə/, e.g., 'royal', 'employer'), /əʊə/ (from /əʊ/ + /ə/, e.g., 'lower', 'slower'), and /aʊə/ (from /aʊ/ + /ə/, e.g., 'power', 'hour').
keyPoints: /eɪə/: player, prayer, layer
/aɪə/: fire, liar, higher
/ɔɪə/: loyal, royal, destroyer
/əʊə/: lower, mower, slower
/aʊə/: power, hour, flower
questions.explanation: In fast conversational speech, English speakers often simplify /aɪə/ and /aʊə/ into long monophthongs like [aː], a process known as smoothing.

questions.question: Compare monophthongs, diphthongs, and triphthongs in terms of tongue movement and vowel stability.
questions.directAnswer: Monophthongs stay in one fixed position (pure); diphthongs glide across two positions; triphthongs glide across three positions within one syllable.
questions.vivaAnswer: Monophthongs are acoustically stable vowels where the tongue and lips remain fixed in one position throughout production (12 in RP). Diphthongs involve an articulatory glide between two distinct vowel qualities within a single syllable (8 in RP). Triphthongs are the most complex, involving a continuous glide across three vowel qualities ending in schwa (5 in English).
keyPoints: Monophthong: 1 static target, pure vowel, constant quality (12 in RP)
Diphthong: 2 targets, gliding vowel, dynamic quality (8 in RP)
Triphthong: 3 targets, complex glide (closing diphthong + schwa, 5 in RP)
All function as single syllabic nuclei
questions.explanation: This comparison illustrates the spectrum of vocalic complexity. In all three categories, the entire sound constitutes just one syllable peak.

questions.question: What is a consonant and how does it differ fundamentally from a vowel?
questions.directAnswer: A consonant is a speech sound produced with partial or complete obstruction of the vocal tract, typically forming syllable margins.
questions.vivaAnswer: A consonant is a speech sound produced when the airstream is obstructed, constricted, or diverted by the vocal tract organs (such as the lips, teeth, tongue, or palate). It differs fundamentally from a vowel, which has completely unobstructed airflow, and phonologically, consonants typically occupy syllable onsets and codas rather than the syllable nucleus.
keyPoints: Produced with complete or partial airflow obstruction
Can be voiced or voiceless (vowels are all voiced in English)
Occupies syllable margins (onset and coda)
English has 24 consonant phonemes
questions.explanation: Obstruction can be total (as in plosives /p, t, k/), partial causing friction (fricatives /s, f/), or diverted through the nasal cavity (nasals /m, n, ŋ/).

questions.question: What three parameters are used to classify and describe any English consonant sound?
questions.directAnswer: Consonants are described by: (1) Voicing, (2) Place of articulation, and (3) Manner of articulation.
questions.vivaAnswer: Every English consonant is classified according to a three-term articulatory label: state of the glottis (voicing: voiced or voiceless), place of articulation (where the obstruction occurs in the vocal tract), and manner of articulation (how the airstream is obstructed or released).
keyPoints: Voicing: vocal cord vibration (voiced vs voiceless)
Place of articulation: anatomical point of constriction (8 places)
Manner of articulation: nature of airstream restriction (6 manners)
Standard viva formula: Voicing + Place + Manner (e.g. Voiced bilabial plosive = /b/)
questions.explanation: Mastering the three-term description is the most essential skill in a phonetics viva. For example, /s/ is a voiceless alveolar fricative; /m/ is a voiced bilabial nasal.

questions.question: Explain the distinction between voiced and voiceless consonants with English examples.
questions.directAnswer: Voiced sounds involve vocal cord vibration (15 consonants), while voiceless sounds do not (9 consonants).
questions.vivaAnswer: Voiced consonants are produced when the vocal cords (vocal folds) are held close together and vibrate as air passes through them, whereas voiceless consonants are produced when the vocal cords are drawn apart, allowing air to pass freely without vibration. English has 15 voiced consonants (like /b, d, ɡ, z, m/) and 9 voiceless consonants (like /p, t, k, s, f/).
keyPoints: Voiced: vocal folds vibrate (15 phonemes: /b, d, ɡ, v, ð, z, ʒ, dʒ, m, n, ŋ, l, r, j, w/)
Voiceless: vocal folds open, no vibration (9 phonemes: /p, t, k, f, θ, s, ʃ, tʃ, h/)
Demonstrated by tactile check: feeling vibration on the larynx ('Adam's apple')
Forms 8 voiced/voiceless pairs (e.g., /p-b, t-d, k-ɡ, f-v, θ-ð, s-z, ʃ-ʒ, tʃ-dʒ/)
questions.explanation: You can test voicing by putting fingers on your throat: /z/ produces continuous buzzing vibration, while /s/ produces only airflow friction.

questions.question: What are the 8 places of articulation for English consonants?
questions.directAnswer: The 8 places are: bilabial, labiodental, dental, alveolar, post-alveolar, palatal, velar, and glottal.
questions.vivaAnswer: English consonants are produced across 8 anatomical places of articulation: Bilabial (both lips: /p, b, m, w/), Labiodental (lower lip and upper teeth: /f, v/), Dental (tongue tip and upper teeth: /θ, ð/), Alveolar (tongue tip/blade and alveolar ridge: /t, d, s, z, n, l, r/), Post-alveolar (just behind alveolar ridge: /ʃ, ʒ, tʃ, dʒ/), Palatal (hard palate: /j/), Velar (soft palate: /k, ɡ, ŋ, w/), and Glottal (vocal cords: /h/).
keyPoints: Bilabial: /p, b, m, w/
Labiodental: /f, v/
Dental: /θ, ð/
Alveolar: /t, d, n, s, z, l, r/
Post-alveolar: /ʃ, ʒ, tʃ, dʒ/
Palatal: /j/
Velar: /k, ɡ, ŋ, w/
Glottal: /h/
questions.explanation: These places trace the vocal tract from the front (lips) to the very back (glottis in larynx). Note that /w/ has two places (bilabial and velar).

questions.question: How do dental, alveolar, and post-alveolar places of articulation differ?
questions.directAnswer: Dental sounds use the upper teeth; alveolar sounds use the bony alveolar ridge; post-alveolar sounds use the area just behind the ridge.
questions.vivaAnswer: In dental sounds (/θ, ð/), the tongue tip makes contact with or protrudes between the upper teeth. In alveolar sounds (/t, d, s, z, n, l/), the tongue tip or blade touches or nears the alveolar ridge directly behind the teeth. In post-alveolar sounds (/ʃ, ʒ, tʃ, dʒ/), the tongue blade approaches the region just behind the alveolar ridge heading toward the hard palate.
keyPoints: Dental (/θ, ð/): upper teeth contact ('thin', 'this')
Alveolar (/t, d, s, z, n, l/): bony alveolar ridge contact ('ten', 'sun')
Post-alveolar (/ʃ, ʒ, tʃ, dʒ/): immediate rear of alveolar ridge ('ship', 'church')
questions.explanation: The millimeter-level shifts along the roof of the mouth create distinct acoustic cavities, drastically altering resonance frequencies and frication noise.

questions.question: What are the 6 manners of articulation for English consonants?
questions.directAnswer: The 6 manners of articulation are plosive, fricative, affricate, nasal, lateral, and approximant.
questions.vivaAnswer: Manner of articulation describes how the airstream is obstructed or controlled. English has 6 distinct manners: Plosives (complete closure followed by explosive burst: 6 sounds), Fricatives (narrow constriction producing continuous friction: 9 sounds), Affricates (stop releasing into fricative: 2 sounds), Nasals (complete oral closure with lowered velum: 3 sounds), Lateral (airflow around sides of tongue: 1 sound), and Approximants (frictionless narrowing: 3 sounds).
keyPoints: Plosive (stop): /p, b, t, d, k, ɡ/ (6)
Fricative: /f, v, θ, ð, s, z, ʃ, ʒ, h/ (9)
Affricate: /tʃ, dʒ/ (2)
Nasal: /m, n, ŋ/ (3)
Lateral (approximant): /l/ (1)
Approximant (glide/liquid): /r, j, w/ (3)
questions.explanation: 6 plosives + 9 fricatives + 2 affricates + 3 nasals + 1 lateral + 3 approximants = 24 total English consonants.

questions.question: Distinguish between plosives, fricatives, and affricates.
questions.directAnswer: Plosives involve complete blockage and sudden release; fricatives involve narrow constriction and friction; affricates begin as plosives and release as fricatives.
questions.vivaAnswer: A plosive (stop) involves complete closure of the vocal tract, pressure buildup, and a sudden explosive burst of air (e.g. /p, b/). A fricative involves a narrow constriction through which air escapes continuously with audible friction noise (e.g. /s, z/). An affricate is a two-phase sound that begins with complete closure like a plosive and releases slowly with friction like a fricative (e.g. /tʃ, dʒ/).
keyPoints: Plosive: Total closure → Pressure buildup → Explosive release (/p, t, k, b, d, ɡ/)
Fricative: Narrow gap → Continuous turbulent friction (/f, v, s, z, ʃ.../)
Affricate: Stop closure → Slow fricative release (/tʃ, dʒ/)
Affricates function as single phonemes, not sequences
questions.explanation: In 'church' /tʃɜːtʃ/, the tongue touches the alveolar ridge for a /t/-closure but releases into /ʃ/-friction, forming the single affricate phoneme /tʃ/.

questions.question: What is a nasal consonant and which 3 nasal phonemes exist in English?
questions.directAnswer: A nasal consonant has complete oral blockage while the velum is lowered, allowing air to escape through the nose: /m, n, ŋ/.
questions.vivaAnswer: A nasal consonant is produced when there is complete closure somewhere in the mouth, but the velum (soft palate) is lowered, allowing the voiced airstream to escape freely and resonate through the nasal cavity. English has 3 nasal phonemes: bilabial /m/ ('man'), alveolar /n/ ('no'), and velar /ŋ/ ('sing'). All English nasals are voiced.
keyPoints: Lowered velum opens nasal cavity passage
Complete blockage in oral cavity
3 English phonemes: /m/ (bilabial), /n/ (alveolar), /ŋ/ (velar)
All nasals are inherently voiced in English
questions.explanation: If you pinch your nostrils while saying /m/, the sound stops immediately because the oral tract is closed at the lips and the nasal escape route is blocked.

questions.question: What are approximants and liquids in English phonetics?
questions.directAnswer: Approximants are frictionless vowel-like consonants (/w, r, j/); liquids are the subset including /l/ and /r/.
questions.vivaAnswer: Approximants are consonants produced when articulators approach each other closely but do not narrow the vocal tract sufficiently to create turbulent friction noise; they are smooth and vowel-like (/r, j, w/). The term 'liquids' refers specifically to the frictionless alveolar sounds /l/ (lateral approximant) and /r/ (post-alveolar approximant).
keyPoints: Approximants: articulators narrow without friction (/w, r, j, l/)
Liquids: traditional grouping of /l/ (lateral) and /r/ (rhotic)
Glides (semi-vowels): /j/ (palatal) and /w/ (labial-velar)
Acoustically vowel-like, but phonologically occupy consonantal syllable margins
questions.explanation: Approximants are phonetically like vowels (continuous voiced laminar airflow) but phonologically function as consonants (standing in syllable onsets, as in 'red' /red/, 'yes' /jes/).

questions.question: Why is the consonant /w/ described as a labial-velar approximant?
questions.directAnswer: Because /w/ is produced with two simultaneous articulations: rounding of the lips (labial) and raising the tongue back toward the velum (velar).
questions.vivaAnswer: The consonant /w/ (as in 'wet') is termed a labial-velar approximant because it possesses a double (co-ordinate) place of articulation. During its articulation, two distinct constrictions occur simultaneously: the lips become tightly rounded (bilabial), and the back of the tongue rises toward the soft palate (velar).
keyPoints: Double place of articulation: Bilabial + Velar
Bilabial action: lip rounding and protrusion
Velar action: back of the tongue raised toward soft palate
Categorized under both bilabial and velar columns in consonant charts
questions.explanation: Because neither constriction produces friction, /w/ is an approximant (semi-vowel) closely related to the close back vowel /uː/.

questions.question: Clarify three common consonant confusions: /θ/ vs /ð/, /ʃ/ vs /tʃ/, and the phonemic status of /ŋ/.
questions.directAnswer: /θ/ and /ð/ differ by voicing; /ʃ/ is a fricative while /tʃ/ is an affricate; /ŋ/ is a single phoneme, not /n/+/ɡ/.
questions.vivaAnswer: First, /θ/ and /ð/ are both dental fricatives, but /θ/ is voiceless ('thin') and /ð/ is voiced ('this'). Second, /ʃ/ is a post-alveolar fricative with continuous friction ('ship'), whereas /tʃ/ is an affricate beginning with a complete stop ('chip'). Third, /ŋ/ is a single velar nasal phoneme; words like 'sing' /sɪŋ/ end in /ŋ/ alone, not a cluster of /n/ + /ɡ/.
keyPoints: /θ/ vs /ð/: voiceless vs voiced dental fricatives ('thigh' vs 'thy')
/ʃ/ vs /tʃ/: simple fricative vs complex affricate ('wash' vs 'watch')
/ŋ/: one single phoneme, never pronounced /nɡ/ in standard RP word-finally
/tʃ/ and /dʒ/ are single phonemes despite using two typographical symbols
questions.explanation: Non-native speakers frequently fail to contrast /θ/ and /ð/ or pronounce a hard [ɡ] at the end of 'singing' /ˈsɪŋɪŋ/. Highlighting these distinctions in viva demonstrates solid phonetic mastery.

questions.question: How does consonant articulation correlate with child phonological acquisition in E412?
questions.directAnswer: Children acquire front stops and nasals first (/m, b, p/) and master complex fricatives and liquids (/θ, ð, r/) last due to articulatory difficulty.
questions.vivaAnswer: Consonant articulation directly correlates with stages of child phonological acquisition in E412. Children universally acquire bilabial and alveolar stops and nasals (/p, b, m, t, d, n/) earliest because their articulatory gestures are visible and motorically simple. In contrast, dental fricatives (/θ, ð/), post-alveolar affricates (/tʃ, dʒ/), and liquids (/r, l/) require fine motor coordination and are acquired much later, often undergoing phonological reduction processes like stopping or gliding.
keyPoints: Early acquired consonants: bilabials and stops (/p, b, m, d/)
Late acquired consonants: dental fricatives (/θ, ð/) and liquids (/r, l/)
Child substitution processes: Stopping (e.g. 'this' → [dɪs]) and Gliding (e.g. 'red' → [wed])
Parallels Jakobson's universal phonological acquisition hierarchy
questions.explanation: This links directly to Jakobson's theory that sounds involving simple binary contrasts (stop vs nasal) precede complex friction contrasts in child developmental linguistics.

questions.question: What is a syllable?
questions.directAnswer: A syllable is a unit of pronunciation containing one peak of sonority (typically a vowel), functioning as a rhythmic beat.
questions.vivaAnswer: A syllable is a fundamental unit of spoken language consisting of a single continuous pulse of sonority or auditory prominence. In everyday terms, it is a rhythmic 'beat' in a word (e.g. 'wa-ter' has two syllables; 'strength' has one), centered around an obligatory vowel nucleus or syllabic consonant.
keyPoints: Unit of pronunciation organized around one sonority peak
Forms the rhythmic pulse or 'beat' of speech
Must contain a vowel nucleus or a syllabic consonant
Spoken syllable count often differs from written letter count
questions.explanation: A syllable is an auditory, phonological reality. For example, 'cake' /keɪk/ has 4 letters in spelling but represents only one syllable because it has a single vowel nucleus /eɪ/.

questions.question: What is the phonetic definition of a syllable and what is the Sonority Sequencing Principle?
questions.directAnswer: Phonetically, a syllable is a sonority peak; the Sonority Sequencing Principle states sonority must rise toward the nucleus and fall toward the margins.
questions.vivaAnswer: Phonetically, a syllable is defined by sonority—the intrinsic acoustic loudness and carrying power of speech sounds. According to the Sonority Sequencing Principle (SSP), sounds within a syllable must increase in sonority from the onset up to the central peak (vowel nucleus), and subsequently decrease in sonority through the coda.
keyPoints: Phonetic definition based on acoustic sonority/loudness peaks
Sonority Hierarchy: Vowels > Glides > Liquids (/l, r/) > Nasals > Fricatives > Plosives
Sonority Sequencing Principle (SSP): sonority rises to peak and falls toward edges
Syllable boundaries correspond to minimum sonority troughs
questions.explanation: In 'plant' /plɑːnt/, sonority starts low with plosive /p/, rises through liquid /l/, peaks at vowel /ɑː/, falls to nasal /n/, and drops to lowest at stop /t/.

questions.question: What is the phonological definition of a syllable?
questions.directAnswer: Phonologically, a syllable is an abstract structural unit that regulates phonotactic sound combinations and stress placement.
questions.vivaAnswer: Phonologically, a syllable is an abstract structural organizing unit within the sound system. It defines the hierarchical constraints governing how consonant and vowel phonemes can legitimately combine in a language (phonotactics), and serves as the domain for prosodic rules such as stress assignment and tone association.
keyPoints: Abstract structural unit of phonological hierarchy
Defines permissible phonotactic combinations (C and V patterns)
Carrier domain for suprasegmental features (stress, pitch, tone)
Hierarchical constituent: Syllable (σ) divides into Onset and Rhyme
questions.explanation: While phonetics treats the syllable as a physical breath pulse or acoustic peak, phonology views it as a structural template (e.g. CV, CVC) governed by grammar.

questions.question: Describe the internal hierarchical structure of a syllable: onset, rhyme, nucleus, and coda.
questions.directAnswer: A syllable (σ) branches into an Onset (initial consonants) and a Rhyme, which branches into a Nucleus (vowel peak) and a Coda (final consonants).
questions.vivaAnswer: A syllable (σ) has a hierarchical structure. It splits into two immediate constituents: the Onset (optional initial consonants) and the Rhyme. The Rhyme then subdivides into the Nucleus (the obligatory vocalic core) and the Coda (optional terminating consonants). The nucleus is the only mandatory element in an English syllable.
keyPoints: Onset: consonant(s) preceding the nucleus (e.g. /k/ in 'cat')
Rhyme: branching constituent containing Nucleus + Coda (/æt/ in 'cat')
Nucleus (Peak): central sonorous vowel or syllabic consonant (/æ/)
Coda: consonant(s) following the nucleus (/t/)
questions.explanation: In 'cat' /kæt/, onset is /k/, nucleus is /æ/, and coda is /t/. In 'string' /strɪŋ/, onset is /str/, nucleus is /ɪ/, coda is /ŋ/. In 'go' /ɡəʊ/, onset is /ɡ/, nucleus is /əʊ/, and there is no coda.

questions.question: Distinguish between open syllables and closed syllables with examples.
questions.directAnswer: An open syllable ends in a vowel without a coda, while a closed syllable ends in one or more consonants (has a coda).
questions.vivaAnswer: An open syllable ends directly with a vowel nucleus and has no coda consonants (e.g. 'go' /ɡəʊ/, 'see' /siː/). A closed syllable terminates in one or more coda consonants following the nucleus (e.g. 'cat' /kæt/, 'milk' /mɪlk/).
keyPoints: Open syllable: ends in vowel, coda is empty (e.g. CV, V: 'me' /miː/, 'to' /tuː/)
Closed syllable: ends in consonant, coda is filled (e.g. CVC, VC: 'cat' /kæt/, 'at' /æt/)
English short vowels /ɪ, e, æ, ɒ, ʊ, ʌ/ cannot end an open stressed monosyllable
questions.explanation: In English phonotactics, stressed open syllables require long vowels or diphthongs ('see', 'go', 'now'); short lax vowels like /æ/ require a closing coda ('cat', 'trap').

questions.question: What is a syllabic consonant and when does it occur in English?
questions.directAnswer: A syllabic consonant is a liquid or nasal that forms the nucleus of an unstressed syllable without any vowel, marked with a subscript mark [ ̩ ].
questions.vivaAnswer: A syllabic consonant is a consonant that functions as the sonorous nucleus (peak) of a syllable in place of a vowel. In English, this occurs in unstressed syllables following an alveolar consonant, most frequently involving /l/ and /n/, and occasionally /m/. It is transcribed in IPA with a small subscript vertical stroke [ ̩ ].
keyPoints: Consonant acting as syllable nucleus without a vowel
Occurs in unstressed syllables after elision of weak vowels like schwa
Most common English syllabic consonants: /n̩/ and /l̩/
Examples: 'button' /ˈbʌtn̩/, 'bottle' /ˈbɒtl̩/, 'rhythm' /ˈrɪðm̩/
questions.explanation: In 'button' /ˈbʌtn̩/, the tongue does not release from the alveolar ridge between /t/ and /n/; instead, air escapes through the nose, making /n̩/ the entire syllable peak without an intervening schwa.

questions.question: What are the phonotactic rules for three-consonant onsets in English?
questions.directAnswer: In a 3-consonant onset (CCC-), C1 must be /s/, C2 must be a voiceless stop (/p, t, k/), and C3 must be an approximant (/l, r, w, j/).
questions.vivaAnswer: English phonotactics allows a maximum of three consonants in a syllable onset (CCC-), but under extremely rigid restrictions: the first consonant (C1) must be /s/; the second consonant (C2) must be a voiceless plosive (/p, t, k/); and the third consonant (C3) must be an approximant (/l, r, w, j/).
keyPoints: Maximum onset = 3 consonants (CCC)
C1 = obligatory /s/
C2 = voiceless stop /p, t, k/
C3 = approximant /l, r, w, j/
Examples: 'string' /str-/, 'split' /spl-/, 'square' /skw-/, 'spew' /spj-/
questions.explanation: No other combination is permitted. A word starting with *pst- or *mkr- violates English phonotactics and is impossible in standard English vocabulary.

questions.question: What are the phonotactic possibilities and maximum consonants allowed in an English coda?
questions.directAnswer: English allows up to 4 consonants in a coda (-CCCC), usually created by adding grammatical inflectional suffixes.
questions.vivaAnswer: English permits up to 4 consonants in a syllable coda (-CCCC), which makes English codas remarkably complex compared to many other world languages. Four-consonant codas almost always arise when grammatical morphemes (such as the plural -s or third-person -s) are added to an already complex three-consonant stem coda.
keyPoints: Maximum coda = 4 consonants (-CCCC)
Typically formed morphologically: stem cluster + inflectional suffixes
Examples: 'texts' /teksts/ (-ksts = 4 consonants), 'strengths' /streŋkθs/ (-ŋkθs = 4 consonants)
Contrast with languages like Japanese which allow zero coda or only /n/
questions.explanation: The maximum theoretical English monosyllable is CCCVCCCC, found in words like 'strengths' /streŋkθs/ or 'twelfths' /twelfθs/.

questions.question: Give examples of phonotactic restrictions in English (impossible sound combinations).
questions.directAnswer: English forbids initial /ŋ/, initial /tl/ or /dl/, final /h/, and non-initial /h/ or /w/ in codas.
questions.vivaAnswer: Phonotactic constraints are language-specific filters. In English, forbidden sound distributions include: the velar nasal /ŋ/ cannot occur in onsets (initial position); clusters /tl-/ and /dl-/ are prohibited word-initially; the glottal fricative /h/ cannot occur in syllable codas; and /v, z, ʒ, ð/ never participate in initial three-consonant clusters.
keyPoints: No initial /ŋ/ (makes Vietnamese name 'Nguyen' difficult for English speakers)
No initial /tl-/ or /dl-/ clusters (unlike Nahuatl or Tlingit)
No coda /h/ (always onset-restricted in English)
Voiced plosives cannot follow initial /s/ in an onset (*sb-, *sd-, *sɡ-)
questions.explanation: These restrictions demonstrate that speech production is governed by abstract cognitive phonological rules rather than physiological tongue limitations.

questions.question: List common syllable patterns in English from V to complex clusters with examples.
