questions.directAnswer: Common patterns include V (a), CV (go), VC (at), CVC (cat), CCVC (stop), CCCVC (string), and CVCCCC (texts).
questions.vivaAnswer: English exhibits a wide range of syllable structures: V ('a' /ə/), CV ('go' /ɡəʊ/), VC ('at' /æt/), CVC ('cat' /kæt/), CCVC ('stop' /stɒp/), CCCVC ('string' /strɪŋ/), CVCC ('milk' /mɪlk/), CVCCC ('text' /tekst/), and CVCCCC ('texts' /teksts/).
keyPoints: CV: /ɡəʊ/ ('go')
VC: /æt/ ('at')
CVC: /kæt/ ('cat')
CCVC: /stɒp/ ('stop')
CCCVC: /strɪŋ/ ('string')
CVCC: /mɪlk/ ('milk')
CVCCCC: /teksts/ ('texts')
questions.explanation: This structural flexibility makes English syllables heavy and consonant-dense compared to CV-dominant languages like Spanish or Italian.

questions.question: What are strong and weak forms in English?
questions.directAnswer: Strong forms are full pronunciations used under stress; weak forms are reduced, unstressed pronunciations of function words in connected speech.
questions.vivaAnswer: Strong forms are the full, citation pronunciations of words articulated with full vowel quality when stressed or in isolation. Weak forms are the reduced, unstressed variants of grammatical function words (prepositions, pronouns, auxiliaries, conjunctions) used in connected speech, typically featuring vowel reduction to schwa /ə/ or /ɪ/.
keyPoints: Strong forms: full vowel quality, stressed, citation form
Weak forms: reduced vowel (/ə/, /ɪ/) or elided consonants, unstressed
Applies strictly to grammatical/function words (approx. 40-50 words)
Examples: 'to' strong /tuː/ vs weak /tə/; 'and' strong /ænd/ vs weak /ənd/ or /ən/
questions.explanation: Weak forms are not lazy speech; they are the standard phonological mechanism that produces the natural stress-timed rhythm of spoken English.

questions.question: Why do weak forms occur in English, and which categories of words have weak forms?
questions.directAnswer: Weak forms occur to maintain stress-timed rhythm; they apply to closed-class function words (pronouns, prepositions, auxiliaries, conjunctions).
questions.vivaAnswer: Weak forms exist to support English stress-timed rhythm: because English compresses unstressed syllables between rhythmic beats, grammatical words lose stress and reduce their vowels. They occur exclusively in grammatical function words (closed-class words), including auxiliary verbs ('can', 'was'), prepositions ('to', 'for'), pronouns ('you', 'them'), conjunctions ('and', 'but'), and articles ('a', 'the'). Content words never have weak forms.
keyPoints: Supports stress-timing: keeps time between stresses roughly equal
Restricted to grammatical/function words (closed class)
Vowels reduce to schwa /ə/, /ɪ/, or /ʊ/
Content words (nouns, main verbs, adjectives) NEVER have weak forms
questions.explanation: If a speaker uses all strong forms ('I /aɪ/ want /wɒnt/ to /tuː/ go /ɡəʊ/ to /tuː/ the /ðiː/ shop /ʃɒp/'), speech sounds robotic and unnatural.

questions.question: When MUST a function word be pronounced in its strong form?
questions.directAnswer: A function word must be strong when: (1) phrase-final, (2) contrastively stressed, (3) cited/quoted, or (4) stranded without a complement.
questions.vivaAnswer: A function word requires its strong form in four key environments: when it occurs at the end of a sentence or clause (e.g. 'What are you looking at?' /æt/); when it carries contrastive or emphatic stress ('The present is FOR you, not FROM you'); when it is quoted or cited in isolation; and when an auxiliary verb is stranded by ellipsis (e.g. 'Yes, I can' /kæn/).
keyPoints: At the end of a sentence: 'Who is it from?' /frɒm/ (never /frəm/)
Contrastive emphasis: 'I said AND, not OR' /ænd/
Quoted or in isolation: 'The word of' /ɒv/
Stranded auxiliary in ellipsis: 'Yes, I have' /hæv/
questions.explanation: Examiners love asking this in viva. Notice that 'at' is /ət/ in 'look at him' /lʊk ət ɪm/, but /æt/ in 'What are you looking at?' /wɒt ə jʊ lʊkɪŋ æt/.

questions.question: Give citation strong and connected weak form transcriptions for 6 common function words.
questions.directAnswer: 'to' (/tuː/ vs /tə/), 'the' (/ðiː/ vs /ðə/), 'can' (/kæn/ vs /kən/), 'have' (/hæv/ vs /həv, əv/), 'was' (/wɒz/ vs /wəz/), 'and' (/ænd/ vs /ənd, ən/).
questions.vivaAnswer: Common examples include: 'to' (strong /tuː/, weak /tə/); 'the' (strong /ðiː/, weak /ðə/ before consonants, /ði/ before vowels); 'can' (strong /kæn/, weak /kən/); 'have' (strong /hæv/, weak /həv/ or /əv/); 'was' (strong /wɒz/, weak /wəz/); and 'and' (strong /ænd/, weak /ənd/ or /ən/).
keyPoints: 'to': /tuː/ → /tə/
'the': /ðiː/ → /ðə/ (before consonant), /ði/ (before vowel)
'can': /kæn/ → /kən/
'have': /hæv/ → /həv/, /əv/
'was': /wɒz/ → /wəz/
'and': /ænd/ → /ənd/, /ən/
questions.explanation: In connected speech, weak forms represent up to 80% of function word occurrences in spontaneous English discourse.

questions.question: What is a contraction and how does it differ from elision?
questions.directAnswer: Contraction is a conventionalized, orthographically represented shortening with an apostrophe (e.g. 'don't'), whereas elision is a general phonetic sound deletion in speech.
questions.vivaAnswer: A contraction is a conventional, grammatically codified combination and shortening of two words represented in standard spelling with an apostrophe (e.g. 'I am' → 'I'm', 'do not' → 'don't'). Elision, by contrast, is a natural phonetic and phonological process where sounds are dropped during fluid connected speech, regardless of whether it is written (e.g. 'last night' pronounced /lɑːs naɪt/).
keyPoints: Contraction: conventionalized grammatical form, reflected in writing with apostrophe
Elision: spontaneous phonetic sound loss in speech stream
All contractions involve phonological reduction, but not all elisions are contractions
Examples of contractions: 'we've' /wiːv/, 'won't' /wəʊnt/, 'they'll' /ðeɪl/
questions.explanation: Contractions are recognized as standard informal words in dictionaries; elisions like dropping /t/ in 'next day' /neks deɪ/ are dynamic phonetic adjustments in pronunciation.

questions.question: Define elision in connected speech.
questions.directAnswer: Elision is the total deletion or omission of a speech sound in connected speech that would be present in citation form.
questions.vivaAnswer: Elision is the phonological process whereby a sound that would be present in the careful, citation form of an isolated word is omitted or dropped in natural connected speech. It is an economy of effort mechanism designed to make speech smoother, faster, and more efficient.
keyPoints: Complete deletion of a consonant or vowel sound
Sound present in isolation is missing in connected speech
Motivated by economy of articulatory effort and speech speed
Common in alveolar stops and unstressed vowels
questions.explanation: The speaker leaves out a sound segment entirely without substituting another. For example, in 'hand bag', the /d/ is dropped, yielding /hæn bæɡ/.

questions.question: What sounds are most commonly elided in English? Give specific examples.
questions.directAnswer: The most commonly elided sounds are alveolar stops /t/ and /d/ in consonant clusters, unstressed vowels, /h/ in pronouns, and /v/ in 'of'.
questions.vivaAnswer: The most frequently elided sounds in English are: (1) alveolar stops /t/ and /d/ when flanked by other consonants (e.g. 'last night' → /lɑːs naɪt/, 'next day' → /neks deɪ/); (2) weak unstressed vowels in fast speech (e.g. 'family' /ˈfæməli/ → /ˈfæmli/, 'library' /ˈlaɪbri/); (3) initial /h/ in unstressed pronouns (e.g. 'tell him' → /tel ɪm/); and (4) /v/ in 'of' before consonants ('cup of tea' → /kʌpə tiː/).
keyPoints: Loss of /t/ and /d/ in clusters: 'last night' /lɑːs naɪt/, 'handbag' /hænbæɡ/
Weak vowel syncope: 'family' /ˈfæmli/, 'police' /pliːs/
H-dropping in pronouns: 'give her' /ɡɪv ə/, 'ask him' /ɑːsk ɪm/
Loss of /v/ in 'of': 'cup of coffee' /kʌpə kɒfi/
questions.explanation: Dropping /t/ or /d/ between two consonants is almost universal in rapid native speech. It prevents awkward three-consonant clusters across word boundaries.

questions.question: Define assimilation in connected speech.
questions.directAnswer: Assimilation is the phonological process where a sound changes one or more phonetic features to become more similar to an adjacent sound.
questions.vivaAnswer: Assimilation is the process by which a speech sound changes its phonetic characteristics (such as place of articulation, manner, or voicing) to become more similar to a neighbouring sound. It occurs naturally across word or morpheme boundaries to allow a smoother, more economical transition between articulatory gestures.
keyPoints: A sound modifies its features to match a neighbouring sound
Can affect place of articulation, voicing, or manner
Driven by coarticulation and articulatory efficiency
Subdivided into regressive, progressive, and coalescent assimilation
questions.explanation: Unlike elision where a sound vanishes, in assimilation the sound remains present but transforms into a different phone (e.g. /n/ becomes /m/ in 'ten boys' /tem bɔɪz/).

questions.question: Explain regressive (anticipatory) assimilation with English examples.
questions.directAnswer: Regressive assimilation occurs when a preceding sound changes to match the following sound (the sound anticipates what comes next).
questions.vivaAnswer: Regressive (or anticipatory) assimilation is the most common type of assimilation in English. It occurs when a preceding sound changes its articulation because the vocal organs are already preparing (anticipating) the following sound. For example, alveolar /n/ assimilates to bilabial [m] before bilabial /b/ in 'ten boys' /tem bɔɪz/, and to velar [ŋ] before velar /k/ in 'ten cups' /teŋ kʌps/.
keyPoints: Direction: Sound 1 ← Sound 2 (anticipatory change)
Most widespread form of assimilation in English
Place assimilation is predominant: alveolar stops (/t, d, n/) adapt to following bilabials or velars
Examples: 'that boy' /ðæp bɔɪ/, 'that girl' /ðæk ɡɜːl/, 'good boy' /ɡʊb bɔɪ/
questions.explanation: In 'that boy', the alveolar stop /t/ shifts its place of articulation to bilabial /p/ under the influence of the following bilabial /b/.

questions.question: Explain progressive assimilation with English examples.
questions.directAnswer: Progressive assimilation occurs when a following sound changes to match the preceding sound.
questions.vivaAnswer: Progressive (or perseverative) assimilation occurs when a preceding sound influences and changes the following sound, so that an articulatory feature persists into the next segment. In English, this is seen primarily in grammatical inflections: the regular plural {-s} assimilates to the voicing of the preceding consonant, sounding voiceless [s] after voiceless stops ('cats' /kæts/) and voiced [z] after voiced stops ('dogs' /dɒɡz/).
keyPoints: Direction: Sound 1 → Sound 2 (perseverative change)
Feature carries forward from first sound to second sound
Governs English inflectional morphology: Plural {-s}, Possessive {'s}, Past tense {-ed}
Examples: 'cats' /kæts/ vs 'dogs' /dɒɡz/; 'walked' /wɔːkt/ vs 'bagged' /bæɡd/
questions.explanation: Progressive voicing assimilation in English inflections is an obligatory phonological rule taught in morphophonology.

questions.question: Explain coalescent (reciprocal) assimilation with English examples.
questions.directAnswer: Coalescent assimilation occurs when two adjacent sounds fuse together to create a completely new third sound.
questions.vivaAnswer: Coalescent (or reciprocal) assimilation occurs when two adjacent sounds exert mutual influence on each other and merge into a single, completely new sound that shares characteristics of both. In English, this typically happens when an alveolar stop (/t/ or /d/) or fricative (/s/ or /z/) is followed by the palatal glide /j/: /t/ + /j/ coalesce into affricate /tʃ/ ('don't you' /dəʊntʃuː/), and /d/ + /j/ coalesce into /dʒ/ ('would you' /wʊdʒuː/).
keyPoints: Two sounds fuse into one new composite sound (A + B → C)
Also called palatalization or reciprocal assimilation
/t/ + /j/ → /tʃ/ ('don't you' /dəʊntʃuː/, 'nature')
/d/ + /j/ → /dʒ/ ('would you' /wʊdʒuː/, 'education')
/s/ + /j/ → /ʃ/ ('issue'), /z/ + /j/ → /ʒ/ ('closure')
questions.explanation: In historical sound change and modern connected speech, coalescent assimilation explains why 'picture' is pronounced with /tʃ/ instead of /tj/.

questions.question: Distinguish between elision and assimilation in terms of phonetic outcome.
questions.directAnswer: In elision a sound is deleted entirely (one fewer segment), whereas in assimilation a sound is modified (same segment count, different quality).
questions.vivaAnswer: The essential distinction lies in what happens to the sound segment. In elision, a sound is eliminated entirely, resulting in one fewer phoneme in the utterance (e.g. 'last night' /lɑːs naɪt/ loses /t/). In assimilation, the sound is not deleted; rather, its articulatory features are modified to match its neighbour, keeping the total number of segments unchanged (e.g. 'ten boys' /tem bɔɪz/ transforms /n/ into /m/).
keyPoints: Elision: deletion (0 segments remain for that target)
Assimilation: feature modification (1 segment remains, but altered)
Elision speeds up tempo by skipping gestures
Assimilation smooths gestures by harmonizing articulators
questions.explanation: A student who says 'assimilation deletes sounds' will lose marks in viva. Assimilation alters; elision deletes.

questions.question: Define stress in phonetics and phonology.
questions.directAnswer: Stress is the relative auditory prominence given to a syllable compared to surrounding syllables through greater muscular energy.
questions.vivaAnswer: Stress is the degree of force, loudness, or auditory prominence with which a syllable is pronounced relative to other syllables in a word or phrase. When a syllable is stressed, it is articulated with greater muscular effort from the respiratory and laryngeal muscles, making it sound louder, longer, higher in pitch, and clearer in vowel quality.
keyPoints: Relative auditory prominence of a syllable
Produced by increased muscular effort and breath pressure
Perceived via pitch, loudness, duration, and vowel quality
Transcribed with primary stress mark ˈ and secondary stress mark ˌ
questions.explanation: In 'banana' /bəˈnɑːnə/, the second syllable 'na' is stressed; it stands out prominently against the unstressed initial and final syllables.

questions.question: What are the four acoustic and perceptual factors that contribute to stress prominence?
questions.directAnswer: The four factors are pitch change, loudness (intensity), length (duration), and vowel quality.
questions.vivaAnswer: The four physical factors producing stress prominence are: (1) Pitch change (a rise or fall in voice pitch, which is the most potent cue); (2) Loudness (greater acoustic amplitude and muscular energy); (3) Length (longer duration of the vowel); and (4) Vowel quality (full, clear vowel quality in stressed syllables versus reduced vowels like schwa in unstressed ones).
keyPoints: Pitch: marked change or movement in fundamental frequency (F0)
Loudness: greater amplitude/muscular effort
Length: extended temporal duration
Vowel quality: full peripheral vowel vs. central reduced vowel (/ə/, /ɪ/)
questions.explanation: These four factors work concurrently. A stressed syllable is rarely just louder; it is almost always higher in pitch, substantially longer, and contains an unreduced vowel.

questions.question: Why is pitch movement considered the most important factor in English stress perception?
questions.directAnswer: Psychoacoustic research proves that human listeners perceive pitch changes much more readily than amplitude changes when identifying stressed syllables.
questions.vivaAnswer: Experimental phonetic research (notably by A.C. Gimson and D. Fry) demonstrates that pitch movement is the most powerful perceptual cue for stress in English. An increase in loudness alone is often ambiguous or overlooked by human listeners, whereas a noticeable change in pitch—whether an upward step or downward glide—immediately flags a syllable as prominent and stressed.
keyPoints: Pitch variation is psychoacoustically the most salient cue to stress
Fry's experiments ranked: Pitch > Length > Loudness > Quality
Loudness alone is insufficient to signal stress to native English ears
Pitch movement directly connects word stress to intonational nucleus
questions.explanation: If you pronounce a syllable very loudly with flat pitch, it often sounds strange rather than stressed; shifting the pitch naturally highlights it immediately.

questions.question: Explain the three levels of word stress in English: primary, secondary, and unstressed.
questions.directAnswer: The three levels are primary stress (ˈ, strongest prominence), secondary stress (ˌ, intermediate prominence), and unstressed (no mark, reduced prominence).
questions.vivaAnswer: In English polysyllabic words, three distinct stress levels are recognized: Primary stress (marked by a raised vertical stroke ˈ before the syllable), which is the most prominent syllable with pitch movement; Secondary stress (marked by a low vertical stroke ˌ), which has rhythmic prominence and full vowel quality but no major pitch jump; and Unstressed syllables (unmarked), which often contain reduced vowels like schwa /ə/.
keyPoints: Primary stress (ˈ): strongest peak, carries pitch movement (e.g. /ˈwɔːtə/)
Secondary stress (ˌ): intermediate prominence, full vowel, no major pitch jump (e.g. /ˌiːvæljuˈeɪʃn̩/)
Unstressed (no mark): least prominence, frequently reduced to /ə/, /ɪ/, or syllabic consonants
Tertiary stress is sometimes posited in American structuralism
questions.explanation: In 'photographic' /ˌfəʊtəˈɡræfɪk/, the third syllable 'gra' carries primary stress (ˈ), the first syllable 'pho' carries secondary stress (ˌ), and the second and fourth syllables are unstressed.

questions.question: How does stress differentiate two-syllable noun-verb pairs in English? Give examples.
questions.directAnswer: Two-syllable noun-verb pairs place stress on the first syllable for the noun and on the second syllable for the verb.
questions.vivaAnswer: In English, many two-syllable words that function as both nouns and verbs are differentiated solely by stress placement: the noun is stressed on the first syllable, whereas the verb is stressed on the second syllable. This stress shift frequently induces vowel reduction in the unstressed syllable.
keyPoints: Noun = Initial syllable stressed: ˈrecord, ˈpresent, ˈimport, ˈobject
Verb = Final syllable stressed: reˈcord, preˈsent, imˈport, obˈject
Stress shift often causes vowel reduction: noun 'present' /ˈpreznt/ vs verb 'present' /prɪˈzent/
Functions as a morphophonological word-class distinction
questions.explanation: Examples: ˈrecord /ˈrekɔːd/ (noun) vs reˈcord /rɪˈkɔːd/ (verb); ˈconduct /ˈkɒndʌkt/ (noun) vs conˈduct /kənˈdʌkt/ (verb). This is an essential viva question.

questions.question: What general stress placement rules apply to two-syllable nouns, adjectives, and verbs?
questions.directAnswer: Two-syllable nouns and adjectives are usually stressed on the first syllable; two-syllable verbs are usually stressed on the second syllable.
questions.vivaAnswer: As a general guideline in English: (1) Two-syllable nouns are predominantly stressed on the first syllable (e.g. ˈwater, ˈtable, ˈfather); (2) Two-syllable adjectives are also typically stressed on the first syllable (e.g. ˈhappy, ˈclever, ˈuseful); (3) Two-syllable verbs are most frequently stressed on the second syllable, especially when containing a prefix (e.g. beˈgin, aˈllow, deˈcide, reˈport).
keyPoints: Nouns: first syllable stressed (ˈtable, ˈbutter, ˈmoney)
Adjectives: first syllable stressed (ˈyellow, ˈsimple, ˈfamous)
Verbs: second syllable stressed (arˈrive, proˈtect, reˈceive)
Exceptions exist based on vowel weight (heavy final syllables attract stress in verbs)
questions.explanation: If the final syllable of a two-syllable verb contains a short vowel and no more than one coda consonant, stress falls on the first syllable (e.g. 'enter' /ˈentə/, 'open' /ˈəʊpən/).

questions.question: Explain suffix rules for stress placement in longer English words (-tion, -ic, -ity vs -ate, -ize vs -ee, -eer).
questions.directAnswer: Suffixes -tion, -ic, -ity place stress on the penultimate syllable; -ate, -ize place stress on the antepenultimate; -ee, -eer take primary stress directly.
questions.vivaAnswer: In English derivational morphology, suffixes interact with stress in three distinct ways: (1) Penultimate-stress suffixes (-tion, -sion, -ic, -ity, -ial) attract primary stress to the syllable immediately preceding them (e.g. eduˈcation, eˈlectric, uˈniversity); (2) Antepenultimate-stress suffixes (-ate, -ize, -fy) place stress three syllables from the end (e.g. ˈeducate, ˈrecognize); (3) Stress-bearing suffixes (-ee, -eer, -ese, -ette) attract primary stress directly onto themselves (e.g. employˈee, volunˈteer, Chiˈnese).
keyPoints: Preceding syllable (penultimate): -tion, -ic, -ity, -ial, -ious (e.g., photoˈgraphic)
Third syllable from end (antepenultimate): -ate, -ize, -fy (e.g., ˈqualify)
Suffix itself takes primary stress: -ee, -eer, -ese, -ette (e.g., refuˈgee)
Neutral suffixes (no stress change): -ness, -ful, -less, -ment, -ly
questions.explanation: Neutral suffixes leave the base word's stress unaffected: 'happy' /ˈhæpi/ → 'happiness' /ˈhæpinəs/.

questions.question: How is stress placed in compound words (compound nouns vs compound adjectives and verbs)?
questions.directAnswer: Compound nouns usually take primary stress on the first element; compound adjectives and verbs take primary stress on the second element.
questions.vivaAnswer: In English compounds, grammatical category determines the stress pattern: Compound nouns normally take primary stress on the first element (e.g. ˈblackbird, ˈgreenhouse, ˈfootball), which distinguishes a compound noun ('ˈblackbird' = a species of bird) from a noun phrase ('black ˈbird' = any bird that is black). In contrast, compound adjectives (e.g. bad-ˈtempered, old-ˈfashioned) and compound verbs (e.g. overˈlook, underˈstand) place primary stress on the second element.
keyPoints: Compound nouns: initial stress (ˈteacup, ˈtypewriter, ˈblackboard)
Noun phrase contrast: ˈgreenhouse (glass building) vs green ˈhouse (house painted green)
Compound adjectives: second element stressed (first-ˈclass, cold-ˈblooded)
Compound verbs: second element stressed (outˈrun, underˈline)
questions.explanation: This distinction is widely tested in oral examinations because it demonstrates how stress operates grammatically to disambiguate lexical items from syntactic phrases.

questions.question: What is sentence stress and how do content words differ from function words in connected speech?
questions.directAnswer: Sentence stress assigns prominence to lexical content words carrying information, while grammatical function words remain unstressed.
questions.vivaAnswer: Sentence stress is the rhythmic pattern of prominence assigned across an entire utterance. English maintains a fundamental division: Content words (nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs) carry semantic information and normally receive sentence stress; Function words (articles, prepositions, pronouns, conjunctions, auxiliary verbs) supply grammatical structure and remain unstressed, usually adopting weak forms.
keyPoints: Content words (lexical): stressed (nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs)
Function words (grammatical): unstressed (articles, prepositions, auxiliaries)
Creates English rhythmic alternation between strong beats and weak syllables
Example: 'The ˈteacher ˈasked a ˈquestion' (stressed words: teacher, asked, question)
questions.explanation: Sentence stress establishes the skeleton of English utterance rhythm. The unaccented function words are squeezed rhythmically into the time gaps between stressed content syllables.

questions.question: What is contrastive or emphatic stress?
questions.directAnswer: Contrastive stress overrides default sentence stress to highlight a specific word or contrast opposing ideas.
questions.vivaAnswer: Contrastive (or emphatic) stress is a dynamic prosodic focus that overrides normal grammatical stress rules to draw special attention to a particular word, correct a misunderstanding, or establish an explicit contrast. Under contrastive stress, even normally unstressed function words receive primary stress.
keyPoints: Special prosodic prominence overriding default rules
Used to highlight contrast, correct misinformation, or emphasize intent
Can stress grammatical words: 'The book is ˈFOR you, not ˈFROM you'
Shifting stress shifts meaning: 'ˈI didn't steal the money' vs 'I didn't steal the ˈMONEY'
questions.explanation: In viva, contrastive stress illustrates how suprasegmental phonology directly controls semantics and pragmatics in discourse.

questions.question: What is the primary empirical criticism of the theory that English is a strictly 'stress-timed' language?
questions.directAnswer: Acoustic measurements prove that inter-stress intervals are not strictly equal in physical time, showing stress-timing is a perceptual tendency rather than absolute isochrony.
questions.vivaAnswer: The traditional claim that English is strictly 'stress-timed' (isochronous) has been heavily criticized by experimental acoustic phoneticians (such as Roach and Crystal). Instrumental laboratory measurements demonstrate that intervals between stresses are not physically equal in milliseconds; instead, intervals expand significantly as more unstressed syllables are added. Isochrony is therefore understood today as a perceptual psychological illusion and phonological tendency rather than an objective physical reality.
keyPoints: Empirical phonetic criticism of strict physical isochrony
Acoustic measurements show intervals between stresses vary with syllable count
Stress-timing represents a perceptual bias and phonological compression tendency
Distinction remains useful pedagogically to explain weak forms and vowel reduction
questions.explanation: While English is not physically isochronous, English speakers perceive it as rhythmic because unstressed syllables compress heavily, keeping rhythm perceptually distinct from syllable-timed languages.

questions.question: What is chunking in spoken English?
questions.directAnswer: Chunking is the division of continuous spoken discourse into manageable, meaningful groups of words separated by brief pauses.
questions.vivaAnswer: Chunking (also called phrasing or tonality) is the process of breaking continuous speech into smaller, grammatically and semantically coherent units called 'thought groups' or 'tone units'. Separated by brief pauses, chunking helps the speaker organize ideas and ensures the listener can easily process and comprehend spoken discourse.
keyPoints: Dividing continuous speech into coherent thought groups
Separated by pauses or pitch resets
Facilitates speaker planning and listener comprehension
Transcribed using vertical bar boundaries: | (minor pause), || (major pause)
questions.explanation: Speaking without chunking sounds unnatural and exhausting. For example: | When I arrived at the station | the train had already left ||.

questions.question: What rules or principles govern how speech is chunked into thought groups?
questions.directAnswer: Speech is chunked along syntactic clause boundaries, semantic sense groups, breathing necessity, and communicative focus.
questions.vivaAnswer: Chunking is governed by four primary factors: (1) Syntactic boundaries (clauses, long noun phrases, prepositional phrases); (2) Semantic completeness (each chunk must express a coherent piece of information); (3) Physiological breathing pauses; and (4) Communicative emphasis and speaking tempo (faster speech produces fewer, longer chunks; formal or deliberate speech produces more, shorter chunks).
keyPoints: Syntactic boundaries: between clauses and major phrases
Semantic sense groups: each chunk conveys a unified idea
Tempo dependency: slow speech = shorter chunks; fast speech = larger chunks
Chunking prevents ambiguity (e.g. 'I fed her | cat food' vs 'I fed | her cat | food')
questions.explanation: Incorrect chunking creates bizarre semantic misunderstandings or sounds disfluent. Intonation phrases align heavily with syntactic constituents.

questions.question: Define tone in phonology.
questions.directAnswer: Tone is the distinctive movement or pitch pattern occurring on the most prominent syllable (tonic syllable) of an utterance.
questions.vivaAnswer: In intonational phonology, tone refers to the specific pitch movement—such as falling, rising, fall-rise, or rise-fall—that occurs on the most prominent syllable of a tone unit, known as the tonic syllable or nucleus. Tone communicates grammatical sentence type, speaker attitude, and discourse status.
keyPoints: Pitch movement or contour on the most prominent syllable
Occurs specifically on the tonic syllable (nucleus)
English inventory: Fall (↘), Rise (↗), Fall-Rise (↘↗), Rise-Fall (↗↘), Level (→)
Signals pragmatic meaning rather than lexical dictionary meaning
questions.explanation: The same word 'yes' can convey complete agreement with a falling tone (↘yes), questioning with a rising tone (↗yes), or doubt with a fall-rise tone (↘↗yes).

questions.question: How does tone in intonation languages like English differ from tone in tonal languages like Mandarin?
questions.directAnswer: In tonal languages, pitch changes word meaning in the dictionary; in intonation languages, pitch changes phrase attitude or discourse meaning.
questions.vivaAnswer: In true tonal languages (such as Mandarin Chinese, Thai, or Yoruba), tone is lexical: changing the pitch pattern on a syllable changes the actual dictionary word and lexical meaning (e.g. Mandarin 'ma' can mean 'mother', 'hemp', 'horse', or 'scold' depending on tone). In intonation languages like English, tone operates at the sentence or discourse level: changing pitch does not change the word itself, but signals pragmatic attitude, question status, or focus.
keyPoints: Tonal languages (e.g. Mandarin): lexical tone (changes dictionary word)
Intonation languages (e.g. English): post-lexical tone (changes pragmatic/attitudinal meaning)
In English, /kæt/ is always 'cat' regardless of whether pitch rises or falls
Tone operates over syllables in tone languages, but over intonation phrases in English
questions.explanation: This is a classic linguistics viva question that tests whether the candidate understands the difference between lexical phonology and prosody.

questions.question: What is a tone unit (also called a tone group or intonation phrase)?
questions.directAnswer: A tone unit is the minimal autonomous unit of intonation containing one major pitch movement on an obligatory tonic syllable.
questions.vivaAnswer: A tone unit (also known as a tone group or intonation phrase) is the basic structural unit of intonation in speech. It consists of a sequence of speech sounds that contains exactly one principal pitch movement (one tone), centered on an obligatory tonic syllable. Every spoken utterance consists of one or more tone units.
keyPoints: Basic structural building block of intonation
Contains exactly ONE primary pitch movement (nuclear tone)
Has one obligatory component: the tonic syllable (nucleus)
Bounded by internal pause or pitch step changes
questions.explanation: A tone unit can be as short as a single monosyllabic word ('↘Yes.') or as long as a complex clause ('| When the ˈbell ↘RANG |').

questions.question: Explain the internal structure of a tone unit: tonic syllable, head, pre-head, and tail.
questions.directAnswer: A tone unit consists of an obligatory Tonic Syllable (carrying the tone), preceded optionally by Pre-head and Head, and followed optionally by Tail.
questions.vivaAnswer: A tone unit possesses a four-part hierarchical structure: (1) Tonic Syllable (Nucleus): the only obligatory element, carrying the main pitch movement; (2) Pre-head: any unstressed syllables occurring before the first stressed syllable; (3) Head: the stretch beginning from the first stressed syllable up to (but excluding) the tonic syllable; (4) Tail: any syllables following the tonic syllable up to the tone unit boundary.
keyPoints: Formula: (Pre-head) + (Head) + TONIC SYLLABLE + (Tail)
Tonic syllable is the ONLY mandatory constituent
Pre-head: unstressed syllables before the head (e.g. 'In a' in | In a ˈlittle ↘WHILE |)
Head: from first stress to tonic syllable ('ˈlittle')
Tail: follows the tonic syllable, continuing the pitch glide ('for us')
questions.explanation: Example: | In a (pre-head) ˈlittle (head) ↘WHILE (tonic) for us (tail) |. In the tail, the pitch movement initiated on the tonic syllable is continued.

questions.question: What is the tonic syllable (nucleus) and how is it identified in an utterance?
questions.directAnswer: The tonic syllable is the most prominent syllable in a tone unit where the nuclear pitch movement begins, normally on the last content word.
questions.vivaAnswer: The tonic syllable (or nucleus) is the focal center of the tone unit. It is the syllable that carries the primary pitch movement (tone), produced with maximum perceptual prominence. In neutral English utterances, the tonic syllable defaults to the stressed syllable of the last lexical content word (the End-Weight / Information Focus Principle).
keyPoints: Focal syllable carrying nuclear pitch glide
Most prominent syllable acoustically and perceptually
Neutral default position: stressed syllable of the final content word
Shifts to earlier words to express contrastive or emphatic focus
questions.explanation: In 'She ˈbought a ˈnew ↘CAR', 'car' is the tonic syllable. In 'She ˈbought a ↘RED car (not a blue one)', 'red' becomes the tonic syllable.

questions.question: Name and describe the five primary tones used in English tone units.
questions.directAnswer: The five tones are: Falling (↘), Rising (↗), Fall-Rise (↘↗), Rise-Fall (↗↘), and Level (→).
questions.vivaAnswer: English utilizes five primary nuclear tones: (1) Falling tone (↘): pitch descends, signalling completeness, certainty, and finality; (2) Rising tone (↗): pitch ascends, indicating non-finality, inquiry, or politeness; (3) Fall-Rise tone (↘↗): pitch falls and rises, conveying reservation, partial agreement, or doubt; (4) Rise-Fall tone (↗↘): pitch rises and falls, expressing strong surprise or enthusiasm; and (5) Level tone (→): flat pitch, conveying routine, boredom, or hesitation.
keyPoints: Falling (↘): statements, certainty, completion ('Yes.')
Rising (↗): questions, incompleteness, politeness ('Yes?')
Fall-Rise (↘↗): reservation, 'yes, but...', uncertainty ('Yes...')
Rise-Fall (↗↘): surprise, impression, sarcasm ('Yes!')
Level (→): routine, list recitation, bored indifference ('Yes-')
questions.explanation: Halliday and O'Connor & Arnold codified these five basic pitch contours as the foundational system of English intonational phonology.

questions.question: Does a tone unit always correspond to a grammatical sentence?
questions.directAnswer: No, a single sentence may contain several tone units, and a tone unit can be shorter than a sentence.
questions.vivaAnswer: No, a tone unit does not necessarily equal a syntactic sentence. While a very short simple sentence can coincide with a single tone unit (e.g. | He ↘LEFT ||), a sentence often consists of multiple tone units corresponding to clauses, phrases, or parentheticals (e.g. | When he ↗CAME | I was ˈeating ↘LUNCH ||). Conversely, a single minor word can constitute a complete tone unit (e.g. | ↘YES ||).
keyPoints: Tone unit is a phonological unit; sentence is a syntactic unit
One sentence can have one, two, or multiple tone units
Tone unit boundaries align with communicative chunks, not just full stops
A single word can be an entire tone unit
questions.explanation: Equating phonological units directly with syntactic units is a common error. Phonology and syntax are distinct grammatical modules that interface closely.

questions.question: Define intonation in phonology.
questions.directAnswer: Intonation is the systematic pattern of pitch variation across whole utterances, often called the 'melody' of speech.
questions.vivaAnswer: Intonation is the meaningful pattern of pitch changes and musical variation across a continuous stretch of spoken discourse or entire utterance. Often described as the 'melody of speech', intonation does not change lexical dictionary words, but conveys syntactic structure, speaker attitudes, information focus, and discourse flow.
keyPoints: Pattern of pitch changes across an entire utterance
Known as the 'melody of speech'
Post-lexical suprasegmental system
Functions at grammatical, attitudinal, discourse, and accentual levels
questions.explanation: Even if two utterances have identical syntax and words, varying the intonation contour produces completely different communicative acts (e.g. statement vs question vs sarcasm).

questions.question: What are the four major functions of intonation in English?
questions.directAnswer: The four major functions are: (1) Grammatical, (2) Attitudinal, (3) Discourse, and (4) Accentual.
questions.vivaAnswer: Intonation fulfills four primary communicative functions in English: (1) Grammatical function (distinguishing sentence types like statements vs questions, or separating clauses); (2) Attitudinal function (expressing emotions, politeness, sarcasm, and personal feelings); (3) Discourse function (managing conversation, signaling turn-taking, and marking given vs new information); and (4) Accentual function (placing the tonic syllable to highlight information focus).
keyPoints: Grammatical: marks clause boundaries and distinguishes syntactic mood
Attitudinal: conveys speaker emotions and stance (polite, bored, enthusiastic)
Discourse: manages conversational turn-taking and shared knowledge
Accentual: marks the most important semantic focus with tonic stress
questions.explanation: These four functions operate simultaneously in spontaneous speech. In viva, candidates should name all four immediately.

questions.question: Explain the grammatical function of intonation with examples.
questions.directAnswer: The grammatical function identifies sentence types (e.g. declarative vs interrogative) and marks clause boundaries.
questions.vivaAnswer: The grammatical function uses pitch contours to identify grammatical structure and sentence types. For example, a syntactically declarative sentence like 'You're coming' functions as a factual statement when spoken with a falling tone (↘), but functions as a question when spoken with a rising tone (↗). It also disambiguates non-restrictive from restrictive relative clauses.
keyPoints: Differentiates sentence types without syntactic reordering
Statement (fall ↘) vs Yes/No Question (rise ↗): 'You're ready ↘' vs 'You're ready? ↗'
Demarcates grammatical clauses and tone unit boundaries
Resolves structural syntactic ambiguities in speech
questions.explanation: In writing, punctuation indicates sentence type; in speech, intonation performs that exact grammatical role.

questions.question: Explain the attitudinal function of intonation with examples.
questions.directAnswer: The attitudinal function expresses the speaker's emotional state and personal attitude toward the listener or topic.
questions.vivaAnswer: The attitudinal function conveys how the speaker feels—such as enthusiastic, bored, sarcastic, doubtful, warm, or hostile. The exact same words can carry radically opposed meanings depending on pitch movement: for example, 'Thank you' with a warm low fall (↘) conveys genuine gratitude, with a flat level tone (→) sounds routine or bored, and with an exaggerated rise-fall (↗↘) sounds sarcastic.
keyPoints: Conveys emotion, stance, and interpersonal attitude
Fall (↘) = businesslike, firm, definite
Rise (↗) = polite, tentative, inquiring
Fall-rise (↘↗) = doubtful, reserved, mitigating
Rise-fall (↗↘) = impressed, highly emotional, or sarcastic
questions.explanation: This function connects directly with pragmatics in E405, where intonation indicates the speaker's illocutionary intent beyond literal semantics.

questions.question: Explain the discourse function of intonation regarding turn-taking and given vs new information.
questions.directAnswer: In discourse, intonation regulates conversational turn-taking and distinguishes known (given) information from new information.
questions.vivaAnswer: The discourse function manages conversational interaction. First, it regulates turn-taking: a low fall signals that a speaker has completed their turn, while a rise or level tone indicates they hold the floor or invite a response. Second, it packages information: new information receives a prominent tonic pitch accent, whereas given (already established) information receives lower pitch prominence.
keyPoints: Turn-taking: falling pitch = floor surrender; rising/level = floor holding
Information packaging: New information = high pitch prominence / nuclear accent
Given/old information = low pitch / de-accented
Topic initiation vs topic termination markers
questions.explanation: David Brazil's discourse intonation framework describes falling tones as 'proclaiming' (new information) and rising/fall-rising tones as 'referring' (shared or given ground).

questions.question: Explain the accentual function of intonation.
questions.directAnswer: The accentual function places the tonic syllable to mark the most important information focus of the utterance.
questions.vivaAnswer: The accentual function of intonation works by positioning the tonic syllable (the nucleus) on the most significant word in the tone unit, thereby marking the informational focus. By shifting the tonic syllable, a speaker alters the entire focus of the sentence without changing a single word.
keyPoints: Marks informational focus via tonic syllable placement
Neutral focus: placed on the final content word ('I bought a ↘CAR')
Marked focus: shifted to earlier elements ('↘I bought a car' [not John])
Guides the listener's interpretation of sentence prominence
questions.explanation: Consider 'I never said she stole my money'. Moving the tonic accent to each of the seven words produces seven distinct interpretations.

questions.question: In what sentence types is falling intonation (↘) normally used in English?
questions.directAnswer: Falling intonation is standard for declarative statements, wh-questions, commands, exclamations, and final items in lists.
questions.vivaAnswer: Falling intonation (↘) is the default contour in English for expressing completeness, finality, and certainty. It is normally used in: (1) Ordinary declarative statements ('It's a beautiful ↘day'); (2) Wh-questions ('Where do you ↘live?'); (3) Imperative commands ('Sit ↘down'); (4) Exclamations ('What a lovely ↘house!'); and (5) The final item in an enumerated list ('...and ↘bananas').
keyPoints: Declarative statements: 'He came home ↘'
Wh-questions: 'What's your ↘name?' (NOT rising!)
Commands/imperatives: 'Close the ↘door'
Exclamations: 'How ↘wonderful!'
Finality in lists: 'apples, oranges, and ↘grapes'
questions.explanation: A common student error in viva is assuming all questions take rising intonation. Wh-questions in English normally take falling intonation.

questions.question: In what contexts is rising intonation (↗) typically used in English?
questions.directAnswer: Rising intonation is used for yes/no questions, polite requests, encouraging inquiries, and non-final items in lists.
questions.vivaAnswer: Rising intonation (↗) signals non-finality, incompleteness, social openness, or inquiry. It is standardly used for: (1) Polar (Yes/No) questions ('Do you like ↗coffee?'); (2) Polite requests or invitations ('Could you help ↗me?'); (3) Expressing genuine surprise or encouragement ('↗Really?'); and (4) Non-final listed items to show there is more to come ('I bought ↗apples, ↗oranges...').
keyPoints: Yes/No questions: 'Is it ↗raining?'
Polite requests: 'Would you mind opening the ↗window?'
Non-final list items: 'one ↗, two ↗, three ↗...'
Checking/confirming: 'You're ready, ↗aren't you?'
questions.explanation: Rising intonation leaves the communicative door open, indicating that the speaker invites the interlocutor's contribution or that more information will follow.

questions.question: What communicative meanings are conveyed by a fall-rise tone (↘↗)?
questions.directAnswer: A fall-rise tone conveys reservation, partial agreement ('yes, but...'), polite disagreement, and contrast.
questions.vivaAnswer: The fall-rise tone (↘↗) is one of the most distinctive and subtle pitch contours in English. It primarily signals reservation, doubt, or partial agreement—often implying an unspoken 'but...'. It is also used for polite contradiction, softening criticism, or establishing explicit contrast between two concepts.
keyPoints: Signals reservation or limitation ('It's ↘↗nice...' [but too expensive])
Partial agreement: agreeing in principle but withholding complete endorsement
Polite dissent: softens disagreement ('I'm not ↘↗sure about that')
Contrastive topic: 'I like the ↘↗colour, but hate the design'
questions.explanation: Saying 'He's ↘clever' is a straightforward compliment. Saying 'He's ↘↗clever' implies 'he's clever, but I don't trust him'. This illustrates prosodic implicature in pragmatics.

questions.question: What communicative meanings are conveyed by a rise-fall tone (↗↘)?
questions.directAnswer: A rise-fall tone expresses intense emotion, strong surprise, being highly impressed, or sharp irony/sarcasm.
questions.vivaAnswer: The rise-fall tone (↗↘) is an emotionally charged contour that conveys heightened involvement, intense surprise, enthusiasm, or strong approval or disapproval. It is also frequently utilized by native speakers to express sharp irony or sarcasm.
keyPoints: Strong surprise or shock: 'You passed? That's ↗↘amazing!'
Intense approval or admiration: 'She was ↗↘marvellous!'
Sarcasm or ironic skepticism: 'Oh ↗↘really?'
Infrequent in neutral, objective discourse
questions.explanation: Because it demands substantial vocal energy, the rise-fall tone immediately signals strong emotional commitment or dramatic theatricality.

questions.question: How does intonation alter the communicative meaning of tag questions?
questions.directAnswer: A falling tag expects agreement (statement of certainty); a rising tag seeks genuine confirmation (real question).
questions.vivaAnswer: Intonation completely changes the pragmatic function of tag questions. When spoken with a falling tone (↘), the speaker is confident of the truth and expects the listener to agree ('It's cold, ↘isn't it?'). When spoken with a rising tone (↗), the tag functions as a genuine question where the speaker is genuinely unsure and requests factual confirmation ('It's cold, ↗isn't it?').
keyPoints: Falling tag (↘): expecting agreement / seeking confirmation of obvious fact
Rising tag (↗): genuine question / speaker is uncertain
Identical words and syntax yield opposite pragmatic forces
Classic viva illustration of the intonation-pragmatics interface
questions.explanation: This distinction proves that sentence mood and illocutionary force in English are mediated by intonation contours rather than syntactic structure alone.

questions.question: What is connected speech and how does it contrast with citation form?
questions.directAnswer: Connected speech is continuous natural speech with phonetic modifications; citation form is the isolated, careful dictionary pronunciation.
questions.vivaAnswer: Connected speech is the continuous, fluid stream of spoken language used in natural conversation, where words flow into one another and undergo systematic phonological modifications (elision, assimilation, weak forms, linking). In contrast, citation form is the artificial, careful pronunciation of a word spoken in complete isolation as recorded in a dictionary.
keyPoints: Connected speech: fluent continuous stream, rule-governed modifications
Citation form: isolated, careful dictionary pronunciation
Modifications include weak forms, elision, assimilation, linking
Connected speech is natural native phonology, not 'careless' speech
questions.explanation: Words rarely sound like their citation forms in continuous speech. For example, citation 'and' is /ænd/, but in connected speech 'bread and butter' it is pronounced /ən/.

questions.question: Distinguish between broad (phonemic) and narrow (phonetic) transcription.
questions.directAnswer: Broad transcription / / shows only contrastive phonemes; narrow transcription [ ] uses diacritics to record precise phonetic detail.
questions.vivaAnswer: Broad (phonemic) transcription is written between slashes / / and represents only the contrastive phoneme units of a language, ignoring non-contrastive phonetic details. Narrow (phonetic) transcription is written in square brackets [ ] and uses extensive diacritics to represent exact physical pronunciation, including aspiration [pʰ], dark [ɫ], nasalization, and dentalization.
keyPoints: Broad (/ /): phonemic, contrastive categories, simple and practical
Narrow ([ ]): phonetic, records allophonic variation and exact physical realities
Broad example: /pɪn/ ('pin')
Narrow example: [pʰɪ̃n] (showing initial aspiration and vowel nasalization before /n/)
questions.explanation: For viva exams, broad transcription annotated with connected speech phenomena (weak forms, assimilation, stress) is standard.

questions.question: What is linking in English connected speech?
questions.directAnswer: Linking is the smooth phonological connection of the final sound of one word to the initial sound of the next word.
questions.vivaAnswer: Linking (or liaison) is the phonological process of connecting words smoothly across word boundaries in continuous speech to prevent awkward vocal tract pauses or glottal stops. In English, linking occurs between consonant-to-vowel transitions, vowel-to-vowel transitions (via /r/, /j/, or /w/), and identical consonant transitions.
keyPoints: Smooth transition across word boundaries
Eliminates hiatus (awkward vowel-vowel gaps)
Types: Linking /r/, Intrusive /r/, Linking /j/, Linking /w/
Creates continuous acoustic stream characteristic of native speech
questions.explanation: Without linking, English sentences sound broken and staccato. For example, 'turn off' is pronounced naturally as /tɜːn ɒf/ with smooth resyllabification /tɜː.nɒf/.

questions.question: What is linking /r/ in non-rhotic accents like RP? Give examples.
questions.directAnswer: Linking /r/ is the pronunciation of an orthographic 'r' at the end of a word when immediately followed by a word starting with a vowel.
questions.vivaAnswer: In non-rhotic accents such as Received Pronunciation (RP), the phoneme /r/ is not pronounced word-finally or before consonants (e.g. 'car' /kɑː/, 'far' /fɑː/). However, when a word ending with orthographic 'r' is followed immediately by a word beginning with a vowel sound, the /r/ is pronounced to bridge the words smoothly. This is linking /r/.
keyPoints: Applies in non-rhotic accents (RP, Australian English)
Word ends in letter 'r'/'re' but is silent in isolation
/r/ is articulated when the next word begins with a vowel
Examples: 'far away' /fɑːrəweɪ/, 'her eyes' /hɜːraɪz/, 'four oranges' /fɔːrɒrɪndʒɪz/
questions.explanation: Orthographic justification is the key: linking /r/ only occurs where the historical spelling has an 'r'. Where no 'r' exists in spelling, the phenomenon is called intrusive /r/.

questions.question: What is intrusive /r/ and why does it occur? Give examples.
questions.directAnswer: Intrusive /r/ is the insertion of an /r/ sound between two vowels where no 'r' exists in the spelling, following /ɔː, ɑː, ə/.
questions.vivaAnswer: Intrusive /r/ occurs in non-rhotic accents when speakers insert an /r/ sound between a word ending in an open or central vowel (/ɔː, ɑː, ə/) and a following word beginning with a vowel, even though there is no letter 'r' in the spelling. It arises by structural analogy with linking /r/ to prevent vowel hiatus.
keyPoints: No 'r' in the written spelling
Occurs after vowels /ɔː, ɑː, ə/ before another vowel
Product of phonological generalization from linking /r/
Examples: 'law and order' /lɔːrənd ɔːdə/, 'idea of' /aɪdɪərəv/, 'media event' /miːdiərəvent/
questions.explanation: Because native speakers perceive pairs like 'sofa' and 'driver' as ending in the exact same vowel /ə/, they generalize the /r/-insertion rule across both words when followed by vowels.

questions.question: What are linking /j/ and linking /w/ (glide insertion) in connected speech?
questions.directAnswer: Linking /j/ and /w/ are transient semi-vowel glides inserted between two adjacent vowels to ensure smooth transition.
questions.vivaAnswer: Linking /j/ and /w/ are phonetic glide insertions that bridge vowel-vowel transitions. When a word ends with a close front vowel or diphthong (/iː, ɪ, eɪ, aɪ, ɔɪ/), the tongue naturally introduces a subtle /j/ glide before a following vowel (e.g. 'he asked' /hiːjɑːskt/, 'my arm' /maɪjɑːm/). When a word ends with a back rounded vowel (/uː, ʊ, əʊ, aʊ/), the rounded lips introduce a /w/ glide (e.g. 'do it' /duːwɪt/, 'go away' /ɡəʊwəweɪ/).
keyPoints: Linking /j/ follows front vowels: /iː, ɪ, eɪ, aɪ, ɔɪ/ ('see it' /siːjɪt/)
Linking /w/ follows back rounded vowels: /uː, əʊ, aʊ/ ('two others' /tuːwʌðəz/)
Arises naturally from coarticulatory glide movement between vowel positions
Prevents glottal stopping between adjacent vowels
questions.explanation: These glides are automatic consequences of vocal tract transition from high front or high back postures to subsequent vowels.

questions.question: Analyze the connected speech transcription of: 'I want to go to the shop.'
questions.directAnswer: Citation /aɪ wɒnt tuː ɡəʊ tuː ðiː ʃɒp/ becomes connected /aɪ wɒnə ɡəʊ tə ðə ʃɒp/ via elision and weak forms.
questions.vivaAnswer: In citation form, the sentence is /aɪ wɒnt tuː ɡəʊ tuː ðiː ʃɒp/. In natural connected speech, it becomes /aɪ wɒnə ɡəʊ tə ðə ʃɒp/. Three changes occur: (1) 'want to' undergoes /t/-elision and vowel reduction, fusing into /wɒnə/; (2) the preposition 'to' reduces to its weak form /tə/; and (3) the article 'the' reduces to its pre-consonantal weak form /ðə/.
keyPoints: Citation form: /aɪ wɒnt tuː ɡəʊ tuː ðiː ʃɒp/
Connected form: /aɪ wɒnə ɡəʊ tə ðə ʃɒp/
'want to' → /wɒnə/ (/t/ elided, /uː/ reduced to schwa)
'the' → /ðə/ (weak form before consonant /ʃ/)
Content words ('want', 'go', 'shop') retain full vowels
questions.explanation: This sentence illustrates how unstressed syllables compress around the stressed verbs and nouns in stress-timed English.

questions.question: Analyze the connected speech transcription of: 'Can you give me a cup of tea?'
questions.directAnswer: Citation /kæn juː ɡɪv miː eɪ kʌp ɒv tiː/ becomes connected /kən jə ɡɪv mi ə kʌpə tiː/.
questions.vivaAnswer: The citation form /kæn juː ɡɪv miː eɪ kʌp ɒv tiː/ simplifies in connected speech to /kən jə ɡɪv mi ə kʌpə tiː/. The modifications are: auxiliary 'can' reduces to weak /kən/; pronoun 'you' reduces to weak /jə/; pronoun 'me' shortens to /mi/; indefinite article 'a' becomes /ə/; and preposition 'of' loses /v/ through elision before consonant /t/, merging into /kʌpə/.
keyPoints: Citation form: /kæn juː ɡɪv miː eɪ kʌp ɒv tiː/
Connected form: /kən jə ɡɪv mi ə kʌpə tiː/
'can' → /kən/ (weak form with schwa)
'you' → /jə/ (weak form with schwa)
'cup of' → /kʌpə/ (/v/ elision in 'of' before consonant /t/)
questions.explanation: Notice how all five function words reduce, leaving only the content words 'give', 'cup', and 'tea' with primary lexical prominence.

questions.question: Analyze the connected speech transcription of: 'He must have been working all day.'
questions.directAnswer: Citation /hiː mʌst hæv biːn wɜːkɪŋ ɔːl deɪ/ becomes connected /hi məs əv bɪn wɜːkɪŋ ɔːl deɪ/.
questions.vivaAnswer: In citation form, the sentence is /hiː mʌst hæv biːn wɜːkɪŋ ɔːl deɪ/. In connected speech, it is pronounced /hi məs əv bɪn wɜːkɪŋ ɔːl deɪ/. The changes include: 'he' shortens to /hi/; modal 'must' reduces vowel to schwa and elides final /t/ (/məs/); auxiliary 'have' drops initial /h/ and reduces to /əv/; auxiliary 'been' reduces to weak form /bɪn/; while 'working', 'all', and 'day' retain primary stress.
keyPoints: Citation: /hiː mʌst hæv biːn wɜːkɪŋ ɔːl deɪ/
Connected: /hi məs əv bɪn wɜːkɪŋ ɔːl deɪ/
'must' → /məs/ (/t/ elided in cluster)
'have' → /əv/ (h-dropping + vowel reduction to schwa)
'been' → /bɪn/ (weak form with short /ɪ/ instead of /iː/)
questions.explanation: In rapid speech, multiple auxiliary sequences undergo heavy phonological reduction, clustering around the lexical main verb.

questions.question: Analyze the connected speech transcription of: 'What do you want for breakfast?'
questions.directAnswer: Citation /wɒt duː juː wɒnt fɔː brekfəst/ becomes connected /wɒt dʒə wɒnt fə brekfəst/ via coalescent assimilation.
questions.vivaAnswer: In citation form, the sentence is /wɒt duː juː wɒnt fɔː brekfəst/. In natural connected speech, it becomes /wɒt dʒə wɒnt fə brekfəst/. The standout change is coalescent assimilation: auxiliary 'do' /d/ and pronoun 'you' /j/ merge into the affricate /dʒ/ with vowel reduction to schwa (/dʒə/). Additionally, preposition 'for' reduces to its weak form /fə/.
keyPoints: Citation: /wɒt duː juː wɒnt fɔː brekfəst/
Connected: /wɒt dʒə wɒnt fə brekfəst/
Coalescent assimilation: /d/ + /j/ → /dʒ/ ('do you' → /dʒə/)
Preposition reduction: 'for' /fɔː/ → /fə/
Demonstrates interaction of assimilation and weak forms
questions.explanation: This example frequently appears in practical viva tests to verify whether the candidate can identify coalescent palatalization in action.

questions.question: How do connected speech phenomena link to sociolinguistic variation and accents in E404?
questions.directAnswer: Connected speech features vary across social classes, regional dialects, and degrees of formality, forming major sociolinguistic variables.
questions.vivaAnswer: Connected speech phenomena directly interface with sociolinguistic variation in E404. Features such as rhoticity versus non-rhoticity govern whether linking /r/ exists, while glottal stopping [ʔ] substituting for /t/ (glottaling) and /h/-dropping vary along social class, age, and formality spectra. More casual styles exhibit extensive assimilation and elision, while prestigious or formal styles retain closer approximations to citation forms.
keyPoints: Rhoticity distinction: rhotic accents (General American, Scottish) lack linking /r/ and intrusive /r/
T-glottaling: substitution of [ʔ] for /t/ in clusters is a prominent British sociolinguistic marker
H-dropping: elision of /h/ in lexical words is a working-class dialect marker in British English
Stylistic continuum: casual/vernacular registers maximize elision; formal registers minimize it
questions.explanation: This connects phonology to Labovian sociolinguistics in E404, proving that phonological processes are socially stratified and stylistically conditioned.
